skills.title: Fast and Responsive LumiBot Strategies
skills.description: Load when a LumiBot strategy is slow, scans many symbols or option contracts, needs fast order handling (cancel after N seconds, immediate hedge or pair legs, OTO/OCO/bracket), or when backtests take too long. Covers sleeptime choice, batched data calls, caching, self.indicators, chunked scanners, bounded quote batching and order state machines.
skills.body:
For external clients, load guides with the BotSpot MCP `skills` tool (action=get, name=<skill>). Resource identifiers written as <skill>:references/<file> use name=<skill> and reference=references/<file>. Installed native clients can read the same local reference file. The following is shared authoring guidance; use the tools actually advertised by your client.

# Fast and Responsive LumiBot Strategies

A LumiBot strategy is slow for a small number of reasons: it runs more
iterations than it needs, it recomputes the same thing every iteration, it reads
data one symbol at a time, or it blocks the iteration while waiting on the
broker. This skill shows how to find which one applies and fix it without
changing what the strategy trades.

The rule that governs everything here: **speed changes how data is acquired and
when work happens, never the trading policy.** Keep the same universe order,
thresholds, quantities, formulas, cooldowns, order guards and fallbacks. A
"faster" version that skips symbols, drops a guard or suppresses eligible trades
is a different strategy, not an optimization.

Related skills: `lumibot-api-reference` for exact signatures,
`lumibot-strategy-building` for the overall build and backtest workflow,
`options-strategies` for options-specific logic, `lumibot-indicators` for
indicator details, `lumibot-ai-agents` for AI-agent strategies.

## References in this skill

Load a reference with the `skills` tool (action=get,
name=fast-lumibot-strategies, reference=references/<file>):

| Load | When |
|---|---|
| `references/scanner-performance.md` | A scan over many symbols or option contracts is slow; you need to batch quotes, cut repeated account/order reads, and keep every guard and price fallback intact. Includes the full two-level scan pattern and a verification checklist. |
| `references/quote-snapshot-example.py` | You are adding batched bid/ask reads with `get_quotes`. A complete, bounded, failure-isolating reader to adapt into the strategy file (it is not an installed LumiBot module). |
| `references/fast-order-management.md` | Cancel-after-N-seconds, immediate hedge or pair legs after a fill, late fills during cancellation, duplicate hedge prevention, manual-cancel and restart recovery, broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket. Includes a complete state-machine pattern and the cases to test. |

## Step 1: find where the time goes

Do not guess. Before changing code:

1. Read the strategy (`get_file` on BotSpot) and list what each iteration does:
   how many symbols, how many `get_historical_prices`, `get_quote`,
   `get_last_price`, `get_chains`, `get_greeks`, `get_orders`, `get_positions`
   and `get_cash` calls, and any loops, sleeps or retries.
2. Check the cadence: `self.sleeptime` and the backtest window. Iterations times
   per-iteration work is the total cost.
3. Look at the logs of a real run (`get_backtest_logs`) for repeated work,
   timeouts, retries and skipped-entry reasons.
4. Classify the problem:
   - too many iterations (cadence), go to Step 2;
   - repeated computation, go to Step 3;
   - serial data reads, go to Step 4 and the scanner reference;
   - blocking order handling or missed deadlines, go to Step 6 and the order
     reference.

After the change, run the same backtest window again and compare (Step 8).

## Step 2: choose the right cadence

- Default to `self.sleeptime = "1D"` unless the strategy genuinely makes intraday
  decisions. A minute cadence runs hundreds of times more iterations than daily,
  and every iteration pays for its data reads. Use `"1M"`, `"5M"` or `"15M"` only
  when the logic needs it, and seconds (`"10S"`, `"1S"`) only for live order
  management.
- Minute-level history is limited (often about two years), so minute backtests
  must use shorter windows anyway.
- `sleeptime` is the gap after an iteration finishes. It never interrupts a
  running iteration. A one-second sleeptime does nothing for a scan that takes
  six seconds; the scan itself has to get shorter or be split (Step 5).
- Work that only needs to happen once a day belongs in `before_market_opens`
  (watchlists, chain lookups, daily resets), with the results stored in
  `self.vars`. It should not run on every intraday iteration.
- Crypto strategies run around the clock with `set_market("24/7")`, which also
  multiplies iterations. Pick the slowest cadence the logic tolerates.

## Step 3: stop recomputing the same thing

**Indicators.** Hand-rolled rolling windows recompute the entire history every
iteration:

```python
# Slow: recomputes the whole series on every iteration
df = self.get_historical_prices(asset, 300, "day").df
sma = df["close"].rolling(200).mean().iloc[-1]

# Fast: computed once over the series, cached, looked up per bar
sma = self.indicators.sma(asset, length=200, timestep="day")
if sma is None or pd.isna(sma):
    return
```

`self.indicators` caches per asset, timestep and parameters, and refreshes
automatically when new bars arrive. For custom math, pass the function to
`self.indicators.custom("label", fn, asset, timestep="day")`; `fn(df)` receives
the full history and returns a Series (scalar result) or a DataFrame
(IndicatorRow result). On indicator-heavy daily backtests this change alone
often cuts runtime substantially. Make the migration behavior-preserving: same
algorithm, smoothing, warmup and decision timing; compare values on a few bars
before replacing an existing calculation.

**Option chains and contracts.** `get_chains` is slow. Cache it once per day (or
per session) in `self.vars`, keyed by date:

```python
today = self.get_datetime().date()
if getattr(self.vars, "chains_date", None) != today:
    self.vars.chains = self.get_chains(underlying)
    self.vars.chains_date = today
chains = self.vars.chains
```

Store the full selected `Asset` objects (strike, expiry, right included), not just
symbols, so later iterations do not refetch or rebuild them. Cache the selected
expiry and strikes and recompute only when the underlying has moved materially
or the date changed.

**Delta hunting.** Never loop `get_greeks()` over a strike list to find a target
delta. Each call is a data request, so a 100-strike loop is 100 requests per
iteration. Use `OptionsHelper.find_strike_for_delta(...)` (keyword arguments,
`underlying_price` required) and `get_expiration_on_or_after_date(...)` with
`underlying_asset=...`.

**Static values.** Levels that should not change once detected (support,
resistance, a pattern's anchor) belong in `self.vars` the first time they are
found. Recomputing them every iteration costs time and makes charts jagged.

**Date math and charting.** Avoid unnecessary date calculations inside tight
loops. Plot price with one `add_ohlc` per bar and indicators with `add_line`; add
markers only for rare events. Markers on every iteration bloat the output and can
break the chart.

## Step 4: batch data calls

Replace per-symbol loops with the batched methods:

| Instead of | Use |
|---|---|
| `get_historical_prices` in a loop | `get_historical_prices_for_assets(assets, length, timestep)` returns `{asset: Bars or None}` and fetches in parallel |
| `get_last_price` in a loop | `get_last_prices(assets)` (trade prices only) |
| `get_quote` in a loop (bid/ask decisions) | `get_quotes(assets)` (LumiBot 4.6.19+), returns `{asset: Quote or None}` |

```python
bars_by_asset = self.get_historical_prices_for_assets(assets, 60, "day")
for asset in assets:
    bars = bars_by_asset.get(asset)
    if bars is None or bars.df.empty:
        self.log_message(f"{asset.symbol}: no bars, skipping", color="yellow")
        continue
    ...
```

Things to know about batching quotes:

- `get_last_prices` returns last trades. It is not a bid/ask snapshot and cannot
  replace a bid/ask or midpoint formula.
- Native batching depends on the data source. Some sources send one request per
  batch (Schwab accepts up to 50 symbols per request); others fall back to
  individual reads. Check before claiming fewer network requests.
- `get_quote` swallows read errors and returns None; direct `get_quotes` can
  raise for the whole batch when one member is malformed or a request fails.
  Wrapping it in `try/except: continue` silently drops healthy contracts. Use the
  bounded, failure-isolating reader in `references/quote-snapshot-example.py`.
- A missing quote stays missing for that scan. Do not let an old helper refetch
  it one by one, which brings the serial loop back.
- Pass the snapshot quote into every consumer that would otherwise fetch again,
  including `OptionsHelper.evaluate_option_market(option, max_spread_pct=..., quote=quote)`.

For live freshness, `get_last_price` and `get_quote` return the latest tick and
are faster than requesting historical bars, which are at best one-minute bars and
can lag. If a live strategy feels sluggish because it calls
`get_historical_prices` for the current price, switch the current-price read to
`get_quote` or `get_last_price` and keep history for indicators.

## Step 5: scanners over many symbols

For a basket scan, split the work into two levels and make each read only where
the original decision needed it:

1. Per symbol, in the original order: keep the symbol-level guard (for example
   an active-order check) exactly where it was.
2. Select candidate contracts from cached chain data, then read their quotes in
   one bounded batch.
3. Evaluate price and eligibility from the batch first. Only for a candidate that
   is still viable, refresh orders and run the original exact-contract guard.
4. Submit using the existing logic and stop or continue as the original did.

This removes both common hot paths (serial option quotes and per-candidate
account reads) without moving guards. The full pattern, the validation and price
fallback rules, and a verification checklist are in
`references/scanner-performance.md`. Read it before editing a real scanner.

When a scan cannot finish quickly (very large universe, slow provider, or an
order deadline in flight), chunk it with a resumable cursor and a wall-clock
budget instead of scanning everything in one iteration:

```python
import time

def _run_one_bounded_scan_step(self):
    universe = self.parameters["symbols"]
    cursor = getattr(self.vars, "scan_cursor", 0)
    budget_seconds = float(self.parameters.get("scan_budget_seconds", 2.0))
    started = time.monotonic()

    while cursor < len(universe):
        if time.monotonic() - started > budget_seconds:
            break                        # resume here on the next iteration
        symbol = universe[cursor]
        cursor += 1
        if self._handle_symbol(symbol):  # existing per-symbol logic; True if it traded
            break
    if cursor >= len(universe):
        cursor = 0                       # full pass complete
        self.vars.last_full_scan_at = self.get_datetime().isoformat()
    self.vars.scan_cursor = cursor
```

Use `time.monotonic()` for elapsed-time budgets. Bound every provider retry per
call and per iteration, and log when a pass was incomplete so nobody mistakes an
unfinished scan for "no opportunities".

## Step 6: fast and safe order handling

The iteration must never block waiting for the broker. Core rules:

- Do not `while`-loop until an order fills, and never use `time.sleep()` (use
  `self.sleep(...)` only for short, bounded waits). Store deadlines and order ids
  in `self.vars` and check them next iteration, or use the resident wait pattern
  in the order reference for second-level deadlines.
- Reconcile pending orders and deadlines **before** starting a fresh scan. After
  submitting an order with a short deadline, return instead of continuing a long
  scan in the same iteration.
- React to fills in `on_filled_order` / `on_partially_filled_order` (the fast
  path), and keep a reconciliation fallback in `on_trading_iteration` for missed
  callbacks. Share one idempotency record keyed by the original order identifier
  so the callback and the fallback cannot both place a hedge.
- Use `self.get_order(order.identifier)` for an exact order. Do not poll it in a
  tight loop, and do not use broad `get_orders()` scans on a deadline-critical
  path. On rate-limit errors (HTTP 429) back off, honoring `Retry-After`.
- `cancel_order` is a request. `CANCELLING`/pending-cancel, a missing read, a
  timeout or a cancel exception are all unresolved, not terminal. Keep the
  affected symbol or pair blocked until the broker confirms a terminal state and
  any required hedge is resolved.
- Use `Order.OrderStatus.ERROR` for rejections; there is no `REJECTED` status.
- Prefer broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket orders when the relationship fits (for
  example take-profit plus stop-loss). Use a strategy-managed state machine only
  for flows a native order class cannot express, such as a custom stock hedge
  after an option fill or a strict cancel-after-N-seconds.
- Second-level deadlines need a continuously running process. On BotSpot, use an
  always-on deployment or a schedule window that covers the whole trading
  period; a one-shot scheduled run cannot own a sub-minute deadline.

`references/fast-order-management.md` has the complete cancel-after-N-seconds
plus immediate-hedge state machine, the deadline architecture, restart
recovery, and the list of cases to test before trusting it with real money.

## Step 7: backtest speed

- Start with a short window (a few months of daily bars) to prove the strategy
  runs and trades, then extend. Long minute-level backtests are the slowest kind.
- Keep the universe as small as the idea allows while iterating; widen it once
  the logic is right.
- Use daily cadence for daily logic. An intraday cadence on a daily idea only
  multiplies work.
- Use `self.indicators`, cached chains and batched reads (Steps 3 and 4). They
  help backtests as much as live trading.
- Avoid live web or API calls in backtests unless they are replay-safe or cached.
- AI-agent strategies call a model on every simulated iteration. They are the
  slowest backtests: keep the first run to about a week of daily iterations and a
  small universe (see `lumibot-ai-agents`).
- Options backtests depend on per-contract data; selecting contracts through
  `OptionsHelper` and caching them avoids requesting data for contracts that do
  not exist or are never traded.
- Log decisions and reasons, but avoid dumping large DataFrames every iteration.

## Step 8: measure and report honestly

On BotSpot:

1. Save the change (`patch_file` or `replace_file`) and read it back with
   `get_file` to confirm every caller uses the new path.
2. Run the same window as before with `start_backtest`, track it with
   `backtest_status`, and compare runtimes.
3. Check `get_backtest_logs` and the trade output (`get_backtest_artifact`,
   `query_csv`) to confirm the strategy still makes the same decisions on the
   same data. Any change in trades needs an explanation.

Report what you measured (runtime, number of requests if logged, iterations) and
describe the saved code accurately. If a hot path is still unchanged, say so. Do
not claim a speedup you did not measure, and never present speed as evidence that
the strategy will make money.

Live deployment and any real-money order always need the user's explicit
approval on botspot.trade. Nothing in this skill is investment advice.

---
name: lumibot-fast-order-management
description: Use when LumiBot strategy code needs fast live order handling, cancel-after-N-seconds logic, immediate hedge/pair/spread legs, manual-cancel recovery, volatile quote handling, or broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket orders.
---

# LumiBot fast order management


When the user asks for a code pattern or minimal state machine, provide a
compact, copyable Python implementation with its callbacks and reconciliation
path. Loading this internal reference does not show that implementation to the
user. Load and adapt the complete combined implementation referenced below instead of replying only with prose.

Choose the responsible mechanics owner. A coupled scan/cancel/late-fill repair
without a safe controller uses the complete fast-order-example implementation;
its own short reservations protect callbacks, polling and broker I/O. An
already coherent complex operation with competing duplicate preparation callers
instead uses `lumibot-strategy-building:references/order-operation-ownership.md`.
Do not mix a new partial state machine or whole-method I/O lock into the complete
controller merely because both resources discuss hedging. Preserve the existing
strategy's actual investment policy in either route.


For a code-pattern or state-machine request, start from the complete combined implementation
referenced below and keep all of its functions: adapt assets, quantities, names and the
user's timeout, but do not write a new state machine from scratch or merge
functions in ways that drop a path. A shorter answer may drop optional
commentary, never a lifecycle path. Before replying, check the fenced Python
against this list:

- Every helper the snippet calls for submit, deadline, cancel, terminal
  clearing, reconciliation and hedging is defined in the snippet. Only the
  strategy's own scan or signal logic may stay a named placeholder, and its
  contract must be stated.
- The entry order id is recorded in the set or dict the callbacks check, and
  the absolute time.monotonic() deadline is the first value computed after
  submit_order returns. Bookkeeping comes after it.
- The wait before cancel dispatch makes no broker request: no get_order and
  no get_orders. In live trading self.sleep(..., process_pending_orders=True)
  only waits; say so in a comment. Preserve a configured full fill-wait
  interval: the optional early-dispatch margin defaults to zero. A request for
  dispatch BY a deadline may configure a measured safety margin; do not silently
  apply that margin to a request to wait the full interval. Keep waits short and
  distinguish local dispatch from later broker acknowledgment.
- cancel_order returns None, not a terminal answer. A broker reply that the
  order already filled arrives as an exception or a fill callback. Wrap the
  call: on an exception, do one exact-order self.get_order(order_id) read;
  FILLED goes to the shared hedge helper, a terminal canceled, expired or
  error state clears the entry, and anything else keeps the blocker armed. A
  successful cancel whose callback never arrives is resolved by one exact read
  on a later iteration.
- One hedge helper serves on_filled_order, the cancel-exception read and later
  reconciliation, fenced by the entry order id. Accepted/submitted/ACTIVE remains
  unresolved until a verified hedge fill fulfills the obligation; cancellation,
  expiry or rejection retains an unfulfilled recovery obligation. State this
  boundary explicitly in a structural answer too. It records a failed or rejected
  hedge as an explicit blocking state and retries it a bounded number of times
  (at least one retry). Only an explicit broker rejection is retryable. An
  exception from the hedge submit_order is UNKNOWN, because the broker may have
  accepted it: keep entries blocked and never resubmit it automatically. A
  hedge order in CANCELLING or PENDING_CANCEL stays active and blocking.
- Every state the code stores is initialized in initialize, and every state
  that can block entries has a path that later clears it or retries it.
- Every exact get_order read is wrapped so a slow, missing or rate-limited read
  becomes unresolved blocking state, never an escaped exception. After a missed
  callback, read the exact order at most once.
- After cancel_order returns, check the local order object for a fill (no
  broker read) and hedge it through the shared helper.
- Finishing a pair never deletes the processed-entry record that the hedge
  fence checks.
- The prose says plainly that sleeptime cannot preempt a running
  on_trading_iteration, and that the strategy controls cancel dispatch but
  cannot guarantee the broker's confirmation latency. It names CANCELLING and
  PENDING_CANCEL as non-terminal and Order.OrderStatus.ERROR as the portable
  rejected state.

For questions about long scans or a slow loop, the answer also covers:
pending-order deadlines run before any fresh scan; after submit_order the
iteration does nothing except the bounded deadline wait and cancel dispatch,
then returns, with no option-chain scans, serial quote loops or hedge
precomputation while that order is pending; preserving the original complete-scan policy while servicing any armed deadline; batched price reads
(get_last_prices, get_historical_prices_for_assets, or get_quotes for bid/ask);
option chains and candidate contracts cached with a bounded TTL; bounded
retries; and callback-first hedging with an exact-order
self.get_order(order.identifier) read as the idempotent missed-callback
fallback.

When saved code with a timed order is "not fast enough" or slow, the order
lifecycle is part of the speed problem, not only the scan. Check the saved code
against the list above and fix every failing item in the same edit: monotonic
deadline, yield after submit, blocker kept through cancel, callback-first
idempotent hedge. Explain the demonstrated lifecycle defects and their effect on dispatch or hedge handling. A fixed limit price alone does not prove why the reported slowdown occurred; describe fill-price limitations separately, without calling an unobserved market price the main bottleneck.
Caching or a faster scan alone is not the repair. Keep the saved timeout, prices
and sizes: shortening the timeout changes the strategy's rules and does not fix
when cancel is dispatched. A "fix it" request authorizes these lifecycle repairs:
save them without asking first. Ask only before changing entry rules or how often
the strategy trades.


For an existing-strategy speed repair, load the complete owner example before
the first saved-file edit. Audit and repair the scan, pending deadline, cancel,
fill and hedge paths together; an early return alone fixes only one symptom.
Use the saved owner integration below when the existing entry/cancel/fill
controller has those coupled defects. A two-line loop/cancel patch is unfinished
while its fill callback still polls before hedging, can hedge twice or never
releases a filled entry. Complete the helper save and entrypoint wiring before
finishing; these are the same requested repair, not optional follow-up work.
When the user requests a fix and that inspection proves a control-flow defect,
save the repair that preserves the existing trading rules. Do not make the user
choose that repair against optional changes to prices, signals or entry frequency.
Those alternatives are not missing prerequisites for fixing the observed bug.
Trace the entire scan loop before describing its entry limit: a pending-order
check before the loop does not stop later loop iterations from submitting and
overwriting that pending order. Repair that demonstrated control-flow defect
under the existing rules before asking about a different trading frequency.
Repairing cancellation and hedging does not authorize more entries. Every
entry caller, including the regular trading iteration and an immediate scan
resumed by a fill callback, must reserve the same entry slot atomically before
broker submission. A broker-list or live-order check is not a reservation: two
callers can both pass it before either publishes its new order. Keep the slot
through uncertain acceptance; release a no-candidate or rejected attempt without
leaving a permanent entry-submitted latch. Preserve a one-shot entry limit or
existing position cap independently of order-state reconciliation. Do not leave cancel/fill races in place because the strategy
has no automatic exit or re-entry policy. Retaining an unresolved entry through
cancel acceptance and fencing its hedge does not add a new trading rule.


Replacing
the broken lifecycle owner is the requested repair, while unrelated trading
policy stays intact. A request for a narrow repair limits the behavior changed;
it does not require keeping an unsafe partial state machine. If the strategy
has a different lifecycle, preserve that contract while applying the ownership
invariants below.
Read back both saved modules before finishing. A helper import without its
complete saved implementation is unfinished; do not replace the copied helper
with an abbreviated local class.

Publishing a fill and reserving its required hedge are one locked transition:
never clear the active entry before the hedge record exists. Keep an already
observed FILLED hedge terminal when `submit_order` later returns; acceptance
must not overwrite a raced fill with ACTIVE. For queue-based fallback hedges,
queue preparation and the entry-keyed submission claim share the same fence.
A later claim cannot undo an extra queue item already appended by a losing
callback. Recheck these three transitions in the final saved code, including
every callback, iteration and recovery caller.



## Preserve one operation through cancellation and hedge failures

Use the complete maintained owner in `deadline-order-example.py`, retaining
its historical entry/alias and per-entry hedge records when integrating it.
A canceled snapshot can clear the active scanning blocker only after the
required reconciliation; it must not delete the historical correlation needed
by a later authoritative fill callback. A callback for that old entry still
reaches the same entry-keyed hedge owner, never the current entry's state.

Before hedge creation, create the owned outcome record. If creation or submit
raises, retain an explicit FAILED/UNKNOWN outcome and its obligation/recovery
policy. A set marking the entry "hedged" plus an exception log is not that
record. Do not fence the obligation away with an untracked placeholder order.

Before the final handoff, trace the original scan/entry/cancel/fill methods and
explain the demonstrated OLD lifecycle defect beside the NEW saved transition.
An acquisition optimization or rotating scan alone does not explain a repaired
cancellation/late-fill/hedge lifecycle. Preserve the original pricing policy.

Use this reference for second-level live order deadlines, immediate hedge legs,
late fills during cancellation, duplicate hedge prevention, manual-cancel
recovery, and broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket orders.

When the user asks for a code pattern or minimal state machine, provide a
compact, copyable Python implementation with its callbacks and reconciliation
path. Loading this internal reference does not show that implementation to the
user. For a new generic deadline-plus-hedge pattern, present the complete tested
class in `references/deadline-order-example.py` with all its method bodies unchanged; explain its input hooks.
Load it with the advertised tool call
`skills reference get(resource_key="lumibot-api-reference:references/deadline-order-example.py")`.
This Python file is registered in the callable resource enum. Loading it is the
same lifecycle implementation task, not an unrelated second reference. Continue
to that exact resource before answering a complete-pattern request; a timing-only
fragment or a claim that the referenced class is unavailable leaves the request
unfinished. Report unavailability only from an actual failed resource read.
A request to show a code pattern requires the actual fenced implementation;
an internal resource filename is not delivered code. Describe the resident
wait accurately: it suspends further scanning in the current iteration while
SDK events are processed; it is not a background or nonblocking worker.
In the explanation, distinguish both external limits explicitly: local cancel
dispatch can be delayed by blocking runtime calls, and Schwab broker cancellation
confirmation latency cannot be promised. A returned cancel request is not
confirmed terminal cancellation.
Do not replace it with a shorter newly invented state machine. Existing saved
strategy repairs must instead integrate only the requested change and preserve
unrelated code. A narrow hedge-observation question may show just that component
without adding new entry/cancel machinery.

Before delivering the complete pattern, audit the emitted reconciliation method
against the maintained class. A due-time check alone is not a finite attempt budget.
Keep its actual refresh counter, maximum attempts, reset/resume policy and visible
blocked exhausted state. An interval-based loop that can read forever omits that
recovery policy even when every individual read is backed off.

## Match the requested deliverable

For an existing-file repair, change only the requested behavior and its necessary
callers. The checks below do not authorize rewriting unrelated strategy logic.
If saved-file readback reveals a specific in-scope defect and editing remains
available, repair it before ending; describing an unfinished repair is honest
but does not fulfill the request. Recheck the initialization, update and reset
callers that own that state, then read back the newest revision.

For a request for a code pattern or state-machine example, minimal means one
clearly defined risk unit, not missing lifecycle code. Provide the necessary
fenced Python together. Implement generic reconciliation, terminal-state and
hedge-recovery helpers that the example calls; a comment saying "reconcile
later" or an undefined `_reconcile_exact_entry_if_due()` does not implement
recovery. Asset selection, signal calculation and strategy-specific quantities
may be explicit inputs. Do not leave the order-management behavior to those
inputs or hide it in an unspecified helper.

- Show a due-time/backoff check and one `get_order(entry_id)` in each later
  reconciliation pass, with unavailable/429/exception results retaining the
  blocker. Both the callback and the actual reconciliation code must reach the
  same entry-id idempotency fence. After cancel dispatch, inspect a locally
  updated filled order or consume its queued callback; an authoritative fill
  does not require another broker read.
- Show why a cancel-pending order remains unresolved. Handle confirmed canceled,
  expired and `Order.OrderStatus.ERROR` results separately from pending/missing
  data. A rejected hedge can be returned as an errored order without raising:
  inspect the returned order as well as catching submission exceptions. Keep
  the original entry's obligation and rejection reason. A saved repair that must
  keep trading needs its actual recovery policy. A conceptual component may
  explicitly retain a visible blocked failure for operator resolution. If you
  include recovery, implement its bounded or operator-requested attempt with
  attributable confirmed zero-fill/preparation-only evidence. Blind retries or
  silently discarded obligations are unsafe. A submitted hedge is not a
  completed pair.
- When scanning is part of the question, show a monotonic wall-clock scan
  budget, a resumable cursor, and caller control flow that exits scanning after
  submitting a timed entry. Mention supported batching for the required data:
  `get_quotes` for bid/ask, `get_last_prices` or
  `get_historical_prices_for_assets` for trade/bar prices. Reuse option chains
  and candidates with a bounded TTL while keeping decision quotes fresh. Keep
  the filled callback fast and exact-order polling as its backed-off fallback.
  `sleeptime` cannot interrupt a running iteration; state this when explaining
  why a deadline can be missed.

## Safety invariants

- Treat an entry, its cancellation, and any required hedge as one lifecycle for
  the risk unit that owns them. Scope blocking to the smallest risk unit allowed
  by explicit strategy and portfolio policy: order, symbol/pair, risk bucket, or
  account. Do not turn one unresolved independent symbol into a universal global
  freeze, and do not let correlated/shared-capital exposure bypass its broader
  risk constraint.
- CANCELLING and PENDING_CANCEL are not terminal. A missing order refresh,
  timeout, rate limit, or cancel exception is also not terminal. Every one of
  those states must keep the entry blocker armed.
- Use Order.OrderStatus.ERROR as LumiBot's portable rejected/error state.
  Broker text may say REJECTED, but generated code must not invent
  Order.OrderStatus.REJECTED.
- A successful cancel_order(order) call does not mean a custom
  on_canceled_order hook already ran. LumiBot queues the strategy callback, so
  it may run just after the current on_trading_iteration returns.
- on_filled_order already carries a filled order. Trust that callback object
  for the fast hedge path; do not make the hedge depend on another
  self.get_order(order.identifier) call that can be slow, missing, or
  rate-limited.
- Callback and reconciliation paths must share one idempotency fence keyed by
  the original entry order.identifier.
- A hedge submission is not a completed pair. Keep the affected risk unit
  unresolved while the hedge is active, rejected, missing, or awaiting a
  bounded retry.
- No timeout, retry count, or blocker scope is universal. Derive each from the
  strategy's stated execution contract, broker capability, and risk coupling.

## Deadline architecture

self.sleeptime = "1S" only schedules the next iteration after the current
iteration returns. It cannot preempt a slow scan. A deadline checked only on a
future iteration can therefore be many seconds late.

A synchronous scan known to occupy that same control path for six seconds
already exceeds a three-second local dispatch budget. State that demonstrated
budget violation directly. Missing broker timestamps may still prevent blaming
the broker or proving the precise cancel-dispatch or terminal-confirmation time.

For a strategy-defined timeout:

1. Finish expensive option-chain, quote, liquidity, and hedge-candidate work
   before submitting the entry.
2. Capture `accepted_at = time.monotonic()` immediately after submit_order
   returns, before bookkeeping, logging or reads. Derive the absolute dispatch
   target from that acceptance time and the user's timeout, subtracting a
   measured local dispatch margin. Store the returned order.identifier.
3. Use a deadline-capable control path that cannot be starved by the next long
   scan. Choose a measured safety margin before the user's actual dispatch
   deadline; do not hard-code one user's timeout into shared guidance.
4. During that short resident wait, process pending events and inspect the local
   tracked order object. Do not call broker-backed get_order immediately before
   the deadline.
5. At the target, call cancel_order once and retain the blocker.
6. Return from the iteration so queued on_canceled_order or on_filled_order
   callbacks can run.
7. If no callback resolves the order, perform one exact-order
   self.get_order(order_id) reconciliation on a later iteration. Back off and
   bound cancel retries.

The timeout is the latest **request dispatch**, not the time to begin waking
up, inspecting state or logging. Waiting the entire timeout and only then calling
cancel_order is already late: local event processing, logging and dispatch take
additional time. Keep a small measured dispatch allowance inside that budget.
For example, a 3.0-second budget with a measured 0.5-second allowance targets
2.5 seconds after acceptance. This is an example, not a new shared trading
policy; preserve the user's fill opportunity and choose the allowance from the
actual path. Do not cancel immediately or hide a missed deadline by skipping an
eligible trade. Include tracking work in the budget rather than resetting the
clock after it. Verify request-start time separately from response-return time.

The strategy can control prompt cancel dispatch. It cannot guarantee Schwab's
network response or broker-confirmed terminal time exactly at three seconds.

A continuous runtime window is sufficient when it spans the strategy's true
operating period and starts immediately when approved inside the window. A
scheduled one-shot process that exits after one iteration cannot own a
sub-minute deadline or callback lifecycle. Persisting ids and deadlines helps a
later reconciliation but cannot replace a live process while an order is
unresolved. If the product has no continuous-window mode yet, `always_on` is the
truthful fallback, not a claim that one daily invocation is equivalent.

"""Bounded public-API quote reads; data acquisition only, never trading policy.

LumiBot 4.6.19+ get_quotes returns exact Asset keys, including None for missing
members. Schwab caps native requests at 50. A failed HTTP request raises
ConnectionError; that type alone does not establish provider-wide downtime.
Malformed members/response contracts can raise ValueError or TypeError during
numeric quote construction. Handle those only at the get_quotes acquisition
boundary; this is not a blanket handler for strategy logic or other exceptions. This
example never calls get_quote as a serial fallback or changes a quote's fields.
It cannot interrupt a blocking broker request. Call it before entering a
short-deadline order lifecycle, or use a provider timeout/control path that meets
the remaining deadline. Acquisition time is not provider quote freshness.
"""

import logging
import math
import time
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Callable

from httpx import HTTPError


QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED = object()


def quote_input(strategy: Any, asset: Any, quote: Any = QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED) -> Any:
    """Preserve a supplied missing quote; only legacy omitted input fetches.

    Adapt an existing price helper's default and acquisition to this pattern,
    retaining its original pricing/fallback calculations after this step.
    None from a snapshot means unavailable, never permission for another read.
    """
    return strategy.get_quote(asset) if quote is QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED else quote


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class QuoteSnapshot:
    quotes: dict[Any, Any]
    unavailable: dict[Any, str]
    acquired_at: dict[Any, float]
    request_count: int


def read_quote_snapshot(
    strategy: Any,
    assets: list[Any],
    *,
    deadline: float | None,
    max_requests: int | None = None,
    monotonic: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic,
) -> QuoteSnapshot:
    """Read once per valid batch; isolate malformed members within a hard budget.

    Pass an actual armed deadline when time-sensitive work can overlap this
    acquisition. An idle pre-entry scan may explicitly pass None: its finite
    contract/request counts and the SDK's finite HTTP timeout still bound work,
    without inventing a quote-age cutoff or a cursor. None is not appropriate
    when a live cancellation deadline needs interleaved service.

    The default request budget derives from the unique contract count: complete
    binary isolation of N members in B initial batches needs at most 2*N-B
    requests. Idle callers should keep that default, not twice the batch count.
    An explicit tighter budget is allowed for an armed deadline; it can leave
    unresolved members that the caller must not call a completed scan.

    The caller owns existing error/retry policy, quote-age validation and order
    management. Inspect unavailable: provider failure, invalid response and
    exhausted budget do not mean that no market or eligible trade exists.
    Missing members remain missing for this snapshot. Isolate a failed batch
    within the same explicit request/deadline budget instead of declaring every
    unrelated instrument unavailable. Budget exhaustion preserves unread work
    as unresolved, not as a completed no-trade scan. Different providers may not implement native batching, so
    measure actual HTTP work before claiming a speed improvement.
    """
    assets = list(dict.fromkeys(assets))
    if max_requests is None:
        batch_count = (len(assets) + 49) // 50
        max_requests = max(1, 2 * len(assets) - batch_count)
    if type(max_requests) is not int or max_requests < 1:
        raise ValueError('max_requests must be a positive finite integer')
    if deadline is not None and not math.isfinite(deadline):
        raise ValueError('deadline must be a finite monotonic time')
    values = dict.fromkeys(assets)
    unavailable: dict[Any, str] = {}
    acquired_at: dict[Any, float] = {}
    pending = deque(assets[index:index + 50] for index in range(0, len(assets), 50))
    requests = 0
    failed_requests = 0
    while pending:
        reason = 'deadline' if deadline is not None and monotonic() >= deadline else (
            'request_budget' if requests >= max_requests else None)
        if reason:
            for batch in pending:
                unavailable.update(dict.fromkeys(batch, reason))
            break
        batch = pending.popleft()
        requests += 1
        try:
            quotes = strategy.get_quotes(batch)
            if not isinstance(quotes, dict) or any(asset not in quotes for asset in batch):
                raise ValueError('Quote adapter omitted requested members')
        except (ConnectionError, HTTPError, ValueError, TypeError) as exc:
            failed_requests += 1
            logging.getLogger(__name__).warning(
                "Quote batch acquisition failed: %s for %d requested assets; bounded recovery applies",
                type(exc).__name__, len(batch),
            )
            if len(batch) == 1:
                unavailable[batch[0]] = ('request_failed' if isinstance(exc, (ConnectionError, HTTPError))
                                         else 'invalid_response')
            else:
                middle = len(batch) // 2
                pending.appendleft(batch[middle:])
                pending.appendleft(batch[:middle])
            continue
        observed_at = monotonic()
        for asset in batch:
            values[asset] = quotes[asset]
            acquired_at[asset] = observed_at
            if quotes[asset] is None:
                unavailable[asset] = 'missing'
    deferred = sum(reason in {"deadline", "request_budget"} for reason in unavailable.values())
    if failed_requests or deferred:
        logging.getLogger(__name__).warning(
            "Quote acquisition: %d failed quote requests; %d retained quotes, "
            "%d unavailable/unread assets; reasons=%s",
            failed_requests, sum(value is not None for value in values.values()),
            len(unavailable), ",".join(sorted(set(unavailable.values()))) or "recovered",
        )
    return QuoteSnapshot(values, unavailable, acquired_at, requests)

A remaining wall-clock deadline, cancel-dispatch reset, callback gated on a later mutable order fetch, or untracked hedge submission means this lifecycle repair is unfinished. Continue the authorized correction; do not final-answer that scanning alone fixed the speed issue. The maintained `deadline-order-example.py` supplies this complete operation; adapt its methods while retaining the strategy's actual entry selection and price policy.


## Explain the causal repair in the final handoff

After a verified saved repair, explain the OLD cause and the corresponding NEW behavior, not just a list of added methods or "a lifecycle problem was fixed." For each demonstrated defect, identify the lost boundary: a long basket iteration could defer the pending cancel; clearing entry ownership when cancellation was merely requested could admit a conflicting entry before confirmation or a late fill; re-reading a mutable order snapshot inside the fill callback could discard that authoritative fill. Explain which of those existed in the inspected file and how the saved changes now preserve the deadline, ownership and one hedge obligation. Keep the original pricing rule and the limit of unverified broker fill latency separate. State what was saved/read back and what execution validation was actually performed. Do not claim a backtest, live deployment or faster fill without that evidence.

## Acquisition-only repair: demonstrated quote/account hot paths

Use the following section with the complete `quote-snapshot-example.py` only when repeated quote/account reads are the demonstrated bottleneck. It changes idle pre-entry acquisition, not the later entry/cancel/hedge owner. Existing timed-order methods alone do not make this scoped acquisition repair incomplete; retain their behavior and do not claim to have qualified their execution. Complete the whole requested operation while
preserving its trading policy. A broad speed request authorizes the coherent
multi-method refactor needed to remove both demonstrated hot paths. A small
helper improvement that leaves the main scan unchanged is unfinished work.

Collect contracts from structural chain data. Keep time-varying order and
cooldown decisions in their original decision phase. Build the quote universe
from the union required by all consumers: a buy cooldown need not exclude that
contract from selling as a hedge. Apply each consumer's own filters when using
the acquired data. A quote fetch moving earlier does not authorize moving or
weakening the order checks. Check a blocker that appears while scanning.
Preserve each original predicate literally when moving acquisition: a bid-based
strike decision must not acquire an additional ask-based filter. Bid and ask
can be crossed in a returned snapshot; batching does not authorize changing
which existing caller accepts it.


## Prepare one coherent repair

For an existing single-file scanner, make the first optimization save in that
same `main.py`: integrate the complete quote reader AND its actual scan,
price/liquidity and preparation callers in one coherent `patch_file` batch.
Include its imports and preserve every unrelated method. An isolated new
`quote_snapshot.py` followed by readbacks leaves the requested scanner unchanged;
do not stage that helper-only write before the primary repair. Preserve an
already modular file layout, but finish the connected primary caller edit in
the same request. A complete reader sitting unused is not a saved optimization.

Collect contracts from structural chain data. Keep time-varying order and
cooldown decisions in their original decision phase. Build the quote universe
from the union required by all consumers: a buy cooldown need not exclude that
contract from selling as a hedge. Apply each consumer's own filters when using
the acquired data. A quote fetch moving earlier does not authorize moving or
weakening the order checks. Check a blocker that appears while scanning.
In particular, do not build a shared snapshot from an entry-only `eligible`
list after buy-cooldown filtering and then reuse it for hedge preparation. Keep
the structural contracts needed by the original hedge cache in the read universe,
even when they cannot be bought now. Missing a still-valid hedge quote can switch
the original option hedge to a stock fallback and changes trading policy.

Before moving a filter into quote preparation, preserve the same field, operator and boundary as the original consumer. An entry predicate using the stock bid is not equivalent to a preload predicate using the ask. Missing sides and crossed bid/ask observations can reach the supported provider adapter; do not assume the usual spread ordering to justify a narrower preload. Build the union using each consumer's original inputs and exclusions, or acquire a broader structural quote universe and retain the original decision filters in their original phase. This is data acquisition work, not permission to add quote rejection or a new trading condition.

Before the first write, trace the full saved file and map these callers:

| Phase | Required data change | Behavior to preserve |
|---|---|---|
| Symbol admission | Keep its current observation/check once per symbol. | Original scope, exceptions, order flags and age rules. |
| Entry scan | Acquire option quotes in supported batches. | Basket order, expiry/strike selection, cooldowns and pricing. |
| Existing viable candidate admission | Refresh orders only where the original decision had an order guard; pass that list through its predicates. | Original exact-contract guard, phase and decision boundary. |
| Pre-entry preparation | Pass the same quote snapshot through every price AND liquidity helper. | Its own candidate universe, formulas and fallbacks; no newly added order filter. |
| After an entry fills | Keep the original fresh-price acquisition and validation. | Existing option-versus-stock choice and order management. |

Prepare all required caller/signature changes together. In a large existing
file, replace complete affected method bodies in one `patch_file` batch rather
than matching repeated state assignments inside them. Copy each method's exact
old body from the current readback. Include its unique `def` line in `oldText`,
or use `replace_range` with verified inclusive `startLine`, `endLine` and
`expectedOldText`. For several ranges, put the lowest method in the file first
so earlier replacements do not shift the remaining line numbers. Include every
required reader, caller and signature change; a helper-only save is unfinished.
A complete `replace_file` containing the current file plus only the scoped
changes is another valid route. Neither mechanism authorizes unrelated edits.
Keep a scan's quote snapshot local and pass it to its consumers when possible;
new persistent state, initialization and reset edits are unnecessary for that.

Cache construction is data acquisition, not a new admission decision. If the
original pre-entry preparation had no account/order read or order predicate,
do not add one there. A transient working order before the fill may disappear
before the original post-fill decision. Removing that contract from the cache
now changes the later option-versus-stock hedge choice, even if scanning is
faster. Preserve the original post-fill fresh checks in their original phase.

Audit every pre-entry consumer of the acquired mapping. A price helper and an
option-market/liquidity evaluator can both issue their own quote request. Pass
the selected snapshot quote through BOTH, including the supported `quote=`
argument of `evaluate_option_market`. A snapshot's explicit missing/None member
must stay missing for that scan; distinguish an omitted optional argument from
a supplied None so it cannot silently trigger a singleton re-fetch.
When the entry scan calls an existing preparation method such as
`_prepare_hedge_candidate_cache`, update that CALL and the preparation method's
SIGNATURE together to carry `quotes_by_asset`. Inside its candidate loop, read
`quote = quotes_by_asset.get(option_asset)` and skip an explicit None before
calling `_get_option_mid(option_asset, quote=quote)` and passing that same
`quote=quote` to `evaluate_option_market` alongside its original arguments.
Updating only the
entry loop leaves the old nested helper on individual requests and can retry
the same acquired missing member. Keep that helper's original formulas,
candidate rules and post-fill fresh reads; this changes acquisition wiring only.

Keep the new reader's actual return type consistent through every caller.
`self.get_quotes(assets)` returns an Asset-keyed dictionary. The complete
`read_quote_snapshot` example returns a `QuoteSnapshot` whose `.quotes` is that
dictionary. Extract `quotes_by_asset = snapshot.quotes` once at acquisition and
pass the dictionary to existing price and pre-entry preparation helpers; those
consumers use `quotes_by_asset.get(asset)`. If an adapted reader itself returns a
dictionary, use it directly. A dictionary has no `.quotes` attribute. Do not mix
the two interfaces between candidate selection and pre-entry preparation.
In final readback, trace the reader's `return` statement and every consumer's
access, including a qualifying candidate that reaches preparation. Compilation
alone cannot detect that return-type mismatch. Correct alternative interfaces
are valid when all their callers agree.

Prefer injecting acquired data into existing helpers over replacing those
helpers or inlining their fields. Before writing, identify each helper's actual
rejection conditions and fallback returns; those are executable policy too.
Keep the measured repair separate from optional extra optimization. If the hot
paths are repeated option reads and per-candidate account reads, retain the
existing one-stock quote call per symbol in its original phase. Complete those
two changes without introducing a basket-wide stock prefetch or changing that
stock helper. One necessary stock read is not the repeated-contract bottleneck.

## Remove both expensive loops

For a broad speed request, inspect the complete nonqualifying path, not only
what runs after a candidate qualifies. Batching only hedge preparation or
reusing one quote after qualification leaves the normal option loop serial.
Batching stocks alone leaves per-option work unchanged.

Separate symbol/phase admission from exact-candidate admission. Retain each
symbol guard in its original position and scope; even an account-wide predicate
may be required once per symbol. Calculate non-mutating price/eligibility
conditions before EXISTING candidate order reads. An ineligible candidate needs
no additional order request. Where the original viable-candidate path had an
order predicate, pass its fresh observation through that predicate. Do not add
an admission predicate to other callers merely because this one needs it. Keep
each original phase's policy and errors unchanged.

```python
# These strategy-local callables represent the EXISTING policies, not new SDK
# methods. Add explicit `orders` arguments to existing predicates where needed.
for symbol in symbols_in_original_order:
    symbol_orders = self.get_orders(statuses=Order.ACTIVE_STATUSES)
    if existing_symbol_blocker(symbol, symbol_orders):
        continue
    # Structural contracts are collected BEFORE any buy-side cooldown/order
    # decision. Derive each consumer's universe independently from that same
    # structural set; an entry-filtered list is not a hedge quote universe.
    structural_contracts = existing_contract_selection(symbol)
    candidates = list(structural_contracts)
    hedge_candidates = existing_hedge_contract_selection(symbol)
    # A buy cooldown can reject an ENTRY without rejecting that contract as a
    # HEDGE. Acquire the union, then retain each consumer's original filters.
    quote_assets = list(dict.fromkeys([*candidates, *hedge_candidates]))
    snapshot = read_quote_snapshot(self, quote_assets, deadline=None)
    for candidate in candidates:
        quote = snapshot.quotes.get(candidate)
        if quote is None or not existing_price_and_eligibility_checks(candidate, quote):
            continue
        decision_orders = self.get_orders(statuses=Order.ACTIVE_STATUSES)
        if existing_candidate_blocker(candidate, decision_orders):
            continue
        submit_using_existing_logic(candidate, quote, snapshot)
        return
```

Trace every helper that calls `get_orders`; passing a list into one predicate
is insufficient if another still refreshes it. An explicit empty list is a
valid observation: use an omitted-input check, not `orders or get_orders(...)`.
Refresh again for the next viable decision. Do not reuse a positive or negative
order observation across later decisions, remove an original guard, or add a
stronger broad-account veto where only an exact-contract guard existed.
For example, an empty order list observed before the first symbol cannot answer
the original guard for the second symbol after quote acquisition: another order
may have become visible meanwhile. Keep the first-level observation per symbol;
remove the redundant per-candidate reads only for ineligible candidates.


## Preserve the existing validation boundary

Batching changes where a quote comes from, not what makes it acceptable. If the
current stock helper requires both bid and ask, pass a supplied quote through
that same helper. Checking only that the Quote object is non-None loses policy.
For a pre-existing two-sided policy, this acquisition-injection illustration
keeps its rejection body unchanged:

```python
def existing_two_sided_quote_check(strategy, asset, *, quote=QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED):
    quote = quote_input(strategy, asset, quote)
    if quote is None or quote.bid is None or quote.ask is None:
        return None
    return quote
```

This is a local helper pattern, not a LumiBot method or a new universal two-sided
requirement. Keep whatever the original helper actually validates. A supplied
quote still runs those checks; explicit None remains unavailable; omitted input
retains the original fresh-read behavior. Do not put validation only inside the
`if quote is None` acquisition branch. An object can exist with one side absent.

For a separate request or profile that actually justifies batching stocks,
retain their checks and use the bounded reader for failed requests there too.
One direct stock-batch failure must not abort healthy later symbols when the
prior singleton path could continue. That additional acquisition change is not
needed to fix an already measured option-and-account-read bottleneck.

## Preserve the existing price policy

Change acquisition while retaining the original valuation branches. Adapt the
existing price helper with `QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED` and `quote_input` from the
complete reader. Only its acquisition/default changes; keep the existing
mid/bid/ask/last-price calculations below it. An omitted quote still fetches for
legacy and post-fill callers; an explicitly supplied `None` stays unavailable.

For an existing caller whose policy is two-sided evaluation followed by its
price-helper fallback, the batched version retains that branch. In this
call-site illustration, substitute the caller's existing spread expression for
`original_max_spread`; it is not a new SDK variable or a new limit:

```python
quote = snapshot.quotes.get(option_asset)
if quote is None:
    continue
# Keep this caller's existing spread parameter and later eligibility checks.
evaluation = self.options_helper.evaluate_option_market(
    option_asset, max_spread_pct=original_max_spread, quote=quote,
)
if evaluation is not None and evaluation.bid is not None and evaluation.ask is not None:
    option_mid = (float(evaluation.bid) + float(evaluation.ask)) / 2.0
else:
    option_mid = self._get_option_mid(option_asset, quote=quote)
```

Use this pattern only where it matches the original pricing policy. Preserve
each caller's later finite/actionability and eligibility checks. Do not replace
a prior fallback with `None`, or derive a new value solely from bid/ask when the
original helper accepted another usable quote field. In the matching Schwab
parser, a quote with positive `lastPrice` and neither bid nor ask can have
`Quote.mid_price` and an actionable evaluation. Missing one side is a different
case; keep the existing evaluation checks instead of inventing a new rule.

Pass the same snapshot into every pre-entry helper, including
`OptionsHelper.evaluate_option_market(..., quote=quote)` on versions supporting
that parameter. A known missing quote must be skipped before calling a helper
whose `quote=None` default would fetch again. After the entry fills, retain the
original fresh-price recheck; do not carry the earlier snapshot indefinitely.
Audit later callers when changing a shared helper's signature.

## Use the complete bounded reader

`quote-snapshot-example.py` is a complete data-read example to adapt into the
saved module/helper. It is not an installed LumiBot import. It preserves exact
Asset keys and quote objects and uses the public `get_quotes` contract.

- Reuse the full `read_quote_snapshot` implementation rather than reimplementing
  its acquisition loop. Log each batch exception before its split/retry branch;
  a successful split does not erase the failed request. Keep `.unavailable`
  reasons scoped to their own assets: skip that candidate and continue original
  candidate traversal using recovered healthy quotes. Do not return from the
  whole scan merely because one isolated member has a non-missing error.
- Use the full reader, including its support types, imports, failure isolation
  and diagnostics. `try: get_quotes(batch); except: continue` can discard a
  healthy qualifying contract when another member makes the parser fail.
- The supported Schwab batch size is 50. For an idle pre-entry scan, pass
  `deadline=None` and omit `max_requests`. The reader computes a finite default
  from unique contracts: at most `2*N-B` requests for full binary isolation of
  N members across B initial batches. Twice the initial batch count is too
  small to recover healthy contracts after a malformed member.
- A returned `None` stays unavailable in this snapshot. A failed request or
  omitted requested key enters bounded isolation/recovery. Do not refetch
  returned missing values through an old helper's implicit singleton fallback.
- On pinned Schwab 4.6.20, `get_quote` catches quote-read/parser failures and
  returns `None`, while direct `get_quotes` can raise. Handle that boundary for
  every newly batched asset type, including underlying-stock prefetch. A
  `ConnectionError` indicates one failed request, not global provider downtime.
- Retain usable members and observable acquisition failures. A malformed or
  failed member must not hide healthy later candidates. Missing quotes, failed
  requests and unread work are distinct; exhausted budgets are not an empty
  market or a completed no-trade scan. Do not introduce an unbounded serial
  fallback or rotate basket priority to conceal incomplete acquisition.

The reader cannot interrupt a blocking HTTP call. An armed cancellation
deadline must be serviced before starting more acquisition, with an appropriate
provider timeout or bounded continuation. A tighter explicit budget may defer
work, but keep unread work explicit. If scanning happens only before submission,
finish that finite idle scan without inventing a deadline or asking the user
to design the batching algorithm.

Reuse structural chain information for a bounded lifetime. Price freshness is
separate: acquisition time does not prove the provider's quote is current.
Keep existing freshness checks and use a new snapshot for a later decision
phase. Do not add a new numeric quote-age filter during a speed-only edit.
Fetch lazily by underlying/bounded step so loading the entire basket does not
delay its first valid opportunity.

## Finish the saved repair before answering

Read the final saved files and trace the full nonqualifying path plus a
qualifying final symbol. Verify both quote and account-read changes in that
readback, every pre-entry consumer, and the later fresh-price callers. Keep
basket priority, expiry policy, thresholds, quantities, formulas, cooldowns,
Rules, dependencies and unrelated files intact. Leave inherited code/Rules
disagreements for a separate user decision.
Compare the old and saved helper bodies, especially deleted rejection and
fallback branches. Review each changed caller with a missing quote, one-sided
quote and newly visible order, rather than only looking for the new batch call.
Verify that failure handling surrounds acquisition and retains healthy members;
a bare batch call or `except: return` is not the original tolerant read policy.

If a hot path remains unchanged, continue the authorized edit. An answer saying
"the main scan is not fully optimized yet" does not complete this request when
supported APIs and ordinary editing tools remain available. Complete the
implementable refactor; report unavailable live timing separately. No live
broker login or forced backtest is needed merely to save that supported edit.

A failed exact-text patch saved nothing, including earlier operations in that
batch. An ambiguous match is an editable local problem, not a permission or API
blocker. Do not retry that same `oldText` in a larger batch. Read the current
file, identify the intended complete method and use its unique method body or
verified range as above; alternatively replace the complete current file.
Continue the authorized repair through a successful save and final readback.
Do not finish with an apology or a request for permission merely because a patch
was ambiguous. Explain a genuinely denied operation, unsupported API or external
prerequisite precisely when it prevents all supported editing routes.
A newly defined reader with its old serial callers still present is unfinished
plumbing. The entry path and pre-entry preparation must actually pass the
acquired quote to their existing helpers, while later callers that omit it
must retain their fresh-read default. Follow the call sites in the saved file;
neither the helper's presence nor an entrypoint readiness result proves wiring.

Measure complete traversal, qualifying decisions, request counts, data age and
cancellation dispatch separately from broker acknowledgment. Report only the
measurements actually observed. A faster-looking change that skips stocks,
suppresses eligible trades, or leaves the demonstrated hot loops unchanged is
not a successful performance repair.

Describe each changed data path precisely in the final answer. A quote snapshot
supplies market prices; order-state checks use their separate order observation.
If those checks still read fresh orders, say so rather than grouping them under
the reused quote snapshot. Verify each claimed change against its saved caller;
an accurate implementation can still be misrepresented by an overbroad summary.

Recommendations are not descriptions of the final saved implementation. Before
claiming when an order refresh happens, inspect its enclosing branch in the
saved caller. A read that still runs unconditionally once per symbol is not a
candidate-only read, even if candidate-only reads were the proposed plan. Say
that repeated reads were reduced unless the more precise placement is verified.
Do not copy a recommendation or revision-analysis description into the final
summary as though it proves the saved call ordering. Report each claimed
mechanism from the actual saved body, including successful alternatives.
