- 🚨 CRITICAL: NEVER use `from __future__ import annotations` in generated code! This import BREAKS backtests and causes the entire strategy to FAIL. Do not add it under any circumstances - it is not needed and will crash the code. If you add this import, the backtest will fail and the code will not run. This is a HARD RULE with zero exceptions.
- 🚨 CRITICAL: Do NOT pass `exchange=` or `currency=` to `Asset(...)`. `Asset` does not accept those kwargs and the strategy will crash. If you need an exchange/venue, pass `exchange=` to `get_historical_prices/get_quote/create_order` (where supported). For forex, represent the pair via the `quote=` argument when placing orders.
- If you are doing minute level backtesting then most users can only go back 2 years maximum, so you should set the start date to be even less than that to ensure the backtest runs (eg. 1 year and 10 months before the current date).
- When trading options, not all strikes/expiries exist. Only call `self.get_chains(...)` when needed as input to an `OptionsHelper` method (expiry selection/validation). Do not manually filter chains to brute-force deltas by looping strikes and calling `get_greeks()` repeatedly.
- Whenever you need to reuse an instrument later (options, futures, even equities), persist the full Asset object. Keeping only the symbol drops strike/expiry/right and other metadata, which forces expensive refetches and breaks cache reuse. Also cache selected expiry/strikes in `self.vars` so intraday retries don’t recompute unless the underlying moved materially.
- CRITICAL FOR OPTIONS: Not all option expiries in get_chains() have tradeable data - many options don't exist yet during backtesting. ALWAYS use OptionsHelper methods (get_expiration_on_or_after_date, find_next_valid_option) which automatically find options with valid data
- CRITICAL FOR OPTIONS: When calling OptionsHelper methods, follow the signature exactly. Use only the documented parameters/kwargs (do not invent args/kwargs).
- CRITICAL FOR OPTIONS: `OptionsHelper.find_strike_for_delta(...)` must be called with keyword arguments and must include `underlying_price` (a float). Never pass `expiry` as the second positional argument.
- When trading options log OptionsHelper.evaluate_option_market(...) results every time and only place orders when OptionsHelper.has_actionable_price(...) returns True; otherwise log evaluation.data_quality_flags and skip so the bot never crashes on NaN/None quotes.
- For options in live trading, prefer SMART_LIMIT to reduce slippage: set `order_type=Order.OrderType.SMART_LIMIT` (defaults to NORMAL) or pass `smart_limit=SmartLimitConfig(preset=SmartLimitPreset.FAST|NORMAL|PATIENT)` to tune. SmartLimitConfig.slippage is BACKTESTING ONLY (fill simulation) and does not affect live orders.
- When you need bracket/OTO exits set secondary_limit_price/secondary_stop_price (and optional secondary_stop_limit_price); do not use the deprecated take_profit_price/stop_loss_price parameters alongside limit_price
- For fast paired orders or timed option cancels, prefer broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket orders when they match the requested flow. If strategy code must manage the pair, use a 1-second cadence, track the submitted order id, poll `self.get_order(order.identifier)` with short `self.sleep(1, process_pending_orders=True)` waits, treat cancel-pending as non-active, and make fill/hedge handling idempotent so callbacks and polling cannot double-submit. `self.sleeptime` does not preempt a running iteration: handle pending deadlines first, return immediately after a timed submit, batch independent prices, cache chains/contracts with bounded freshness, and split large scans into resumable wall-clock-bounded chunks.
- Use components when needed, they're usually good because they have code that has been tested and is known to work well.
- We usually use SPY as the benchmark asset for backtesting unless otherwise specified.
- Do not hardcode backtesting start/end dates in the script. Even when the user asks for a specific date range, BotSpot's backtest tool/environment controls the actual run window so the first test can use a window that fits the rules and any requested run can use its own dates.
- Keep in mind that when you sell an asset you dont immediately get the cash, you wont have the cash until the next iteration
- For live open-order checks, use `self.get_orders(statuses=Order.ACTIVE_STATUSES)`. Do not use raw string status filters.
- When checking duplicate or blocking orders, filter by active statuses and by the exact asset or option contract. Filled, canceled, rejected, expired, or error orders should not block new entries.
- After `submit_order(order)`, broker state may take a short moment to reflect the new order. If checking the same order in the same iteration, call `self.sleep(..., process_pending_orders=True)`, then check `self.get_order(order.identifier)` or filtered `self.get_orders(...)`. Prefer tracking the submitted order identifier.
- Remember that USD is always considered a position, so when you self.get_positions() it will return USD as a position if you have cash in your account (USD is considered a position in the account) Asset("USD", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.FOREX) is the USD position
- Use `deposit_cash()`, `withdraw_cash()`, and `adjust_cash()` for explicit backtest cashflows or broker-like balance adjustments. Do NOT fake deposits or withdrawals by modifying returns, prices, or order fills.
- Use `configure_cash_financing()` and `set_cash_financing_rates()` when the strategy needs margin debit, interest on positive cash, or broker-like financing behavior in backtests.
- Try to avoid using sleep methods in the strategy because they are blocking and can stop important code from running. instead just wait for the next iteration to run and check the time elapsed. Sleep methods are blocking and will prevent the bot from running other code so they should be avoided.
- API keys such as grok API keys should be stored in environment variables and not hardcoded in the code.
- Unless the user specifies otherwise, the default behavior should be to use all the cash in the account for each trade
- When youre looking for an expiration date for options, remember that not all expirations are always available so you might have to look for another expiration thats close by
- Never use datetime.now()! it is wrong, use self.get_datetime() instead
- If someone asks to start a backtest with a certain buget then set the budget in the backtest function like MyStrategy.backtest(budget=the_budget) to that value
- Yahoo backtesting does not support options. For options backtests, prefer datasource_class=None so LumiBot can resolve the configured provider from the environment. If the user explicitly requests a direct provider binding, ThetaDataBacktesting or PolygonDataBacktesting are valid explicit choices.
- When you use get_chains() to get options chains (and you usually should), remember that you're not going to get every possible option expiry so you might have to look for another expiry that is close to the one you want
- Always make sure you give working code, no demo code or pseudo code! Always functional code that can be run as is.
- Backtestable strategy code should trade under realistic default parameters unless the user explicitly asks for rare-event/advice-only behavior. Avoid over-tight filter stacks that produce `completed_no_trades`; log skipped-entry reasons, and never put conditional expressions inside f-string format specs; compute the display value first.
- Use self.vars for variables that need to persist between trading iterations, bot restarts, or between different lifecycle methods.
- In live trading, get_last_price and get_quote pull the broker's latest tick (can lead minute bars); in backtests they fall back to the newest completed bar, and both may be None when feeds are empty.
- When you need historical bars for many symbols, prefer get_historical_prices_for_assets so the batch/threaded fetch keeps things fast and avoids rate limits.
- Add markers/lines/OHLC only when you have valid numeric data; skip plotting when values are missing to avoid chart warnings.
- For bracket/OCO/OTO orders set order_class=Order.OrderClass.BRACKET/OCO/OTO and choose a valid order_type such as Order.OrderType.MARKET or LIMIT (OrderType itself has no BRACKET member).
- Try to use the components provided in the prompt when possible, they are there to help you and have been tested to work well.
- Unless the user explicitly asks for it, don't use if self.first_iteration: in the on_trading_iteration method because most people don't need it.
- Perplexity Helper is very useful when the user wants to do things like stock screening or strategies based on recent news.
- Try to use add_marker, add_line, and add_ohlc whenever it makes sense; they are very useful for debugging and for visualising the strategy. Use add_ohlc for price bars (OHLC candles), add_line for continuous single-value indicators (SMA/RSI/levels), and add_marker for infrequent events (buy/sell signals).
- IMPORTANT: When using add_marker/add_line/add_ohlc, if you have an Asset object for the thing you're plotting, you MUST pass it via the asset parameter (e.g., self.add_ohlc("SPY", open=o, high=h, low=l, close=c, dt=dt, asset=my_asset)). Passing the asset enables proper multi-symbol charting where indicators overlay on their corresponding asset's price chart instead of being separate subplots.
- IMPORTANT: When asset is provided, do NOT set plot_name for normal price/indicator overlays. Let Lumibot group overlays by asset automatically.
- Use plot_name only when intentionally creating a separate indicator pane (RSI/MACD/Stochastic/Volume/etc.).
- Do NOT create per-symbol plot_name values unless the user explicitly asks for dedicated panels.
- Keep the number of distinct plot_name values small by default (max 4) unless the user explicitly asks for more.
- We don't need markers for when we buy or sell something, we already have that in the logs. Markers are to give us extra information about the strategy and to help us debug it, so we should use them for things that are not already in the logs.
- It is good practice to plot price candles whenever you get bars through get_historical_prices(), so you can see how the price is changing over time. This series should be named after the asset (e.g., "SPY" or "AAPL"), and you should pass the asset parameter (e.g., self.add_ohlc("SPY", open=o, high=h, low=l, close=c, dt=dt, asset=spy_asset)). This is very useful when comparing the price of an asset to an indicator or a moving average.
- Try to limit the amount of lines to 3 or 4 unless asked otherwise, it gets messy when we have too many line and marker types
- add_line() and add_marker() both accept a `dt` parameter that can be ANY datetime - past or present. To draw retroactively, either (1) loop over get_historical_prices().df.index for past datetimes, or (2) store datetimes in self.vars as you iterate and loop back when needed.
- PREFERRED CHARTING APPROACH: For most indicators (support/resistance, trendlines, pattern detection, signals), draw retroactively by looping over past datetimes with the dt parameter. This produces cleaner charts. Only use per-iteration drawing for simple deterministic indicators (like EMAs or RSI) that are recalculated fresh each bar.
- When drawing indicators that should stay constant (horizontal levels, detected patterns), LOCK the values in self.vars when first detected. Don't recalculate each iteration or lines will have unwanted peaks/valleys.
- Never get api keys like this "os.getenv('PERPLEXITY_API_KEY', 'your_api_key_here')". if there is no api key is should be None. That way we can warn the user. "your_api_key_here" is not a valid api key and should never be used. Always use os.getenv('PERPLEXITY_API_KEY') or os.getenv('PERPLEXITY_API_KEY', None) to get the api key. If the user has not set the api key then it will be None and we can warn them.
- If a user ever mentioned that they want a bot that automatically rebalances their portfolio then you should consider using the DRIFTREBALANCERLOGIC component. You can set the weights in the component and it will automatically rebalance the portfolio based on those weights.
- Remember that crypto strategies should always set_market("24/7") in the initialize method. For crypto backtesting, prefer datasource_class=None so LumiBot can resolve the configured provider from the environment. If the user explicitly requests a direct provider binding, PolygonDataBacktesting or CcxtBacktesting are valid explicit choices.
- For spot crypto, the `Asset` symbol is the base coin only. Use `Asset("BTC", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO)` with `quote_asset=Asset("USD", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.FOREX)` for BTC/USD. Do not use `Asset("BTC-USD", ...)`, `Asset("BTC/USD", ...)`, or `Asset("BTCUSD", ...)`; the runner will look for a nonexistent `BTC-USD/USD`-style asset and the first backtest can complete with no trades.
- If you want to perform an action "before the market opens", you should use the before_market_opens lifecycle method, and if you need to use any data or results from that step later (e.g., in on_trading_iteration), store it in a persistent variable such as self.vars.
- If you want to perform an action "during trading hours" or "during market hours", you should implement that logic inside the on_trading_iteration lifecycle method.
- Make sure you add lots of logs, they are very useful for debugging and understanding the strategy's behavior. Use self.log_message() to log the inputs checked, the comparison result, and what the bot decided to do.
- Whether you submit, skip, or close an order, log the symbol, side, quantity, and the key signal/value that drove that choice so trade flow is traceable.
- Don't forget that with crypto assets you can buy fractions of an asset, so you can buy 0.5 BTC or 0.1 ETH or 0.01 SOL. This can sometimes also be doen for stocks, depending on the broker.
- If someone metions creating a strategy for Bitunix or crypto perpetual futures, trade `Asset("BTCUSDT", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO_FUTURE)` (or ETHUSDT/SOLUSDT). In backtests, LumiBot uses exact spot history for the same quote asset as the proxy for USDT crypto futures, so `BTCUSDT` maps to `BTC/USDT`, not `BTC/USD`. Keep `assetClasses`/`dataRequirements` as ["crypto"] and use `datasource_class=None`.
- The default quote asset for Bitunix is Asset("USDT", Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO), so either don't set it at all or set it to `quote_asset=Asset("USDT", Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO)` by default.
- For Crypto Futures assets (such as with Bitunix), you need to close positions using self.close_position() instead of like normally submit_order(). With Bitunix if you submit_order() it will always open a new position, just on the other side of the trade. So you have to use self.close_position() to close the position and then use submit_order() to open a new position.
- With crypto futures (for example with Bitunix) you have to use both the symbols in the asset (eg. `future_asset = Asset("BTCUSDT", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO_FUTURE)`) because a futures order always needs to know both sides of the trade, so you have to use both the symbol and the quote asset. Another example would be `future_asset = Asset("ETHUSDT", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO_FUTURE)`.
- For live crypto futures, if direct CRYPTO_FUTURE prices are unavailable, read spot with `Asset("BTC", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO)` and place orders with the future asset.
- If anyone ever mentions a broker ignore it. All brokers are handled by lumibot and the strategy code should not handle any broker API keys or anything like that. The strategy code should only handle the strategy logic and not the broker. The broker details are sent as environment variables and completely handled by lumibot. The strategy code should not handle any broker API keys or anything like that.
- Treat on_filled_order as helpful but not guaranteed. Use it when available, but verify live state with self.get_positions() before clearing position/order state.
- For live open-order checks, use self.get_orders(statuses=Order.ACTIVE_STATUSES), not raw string status checks. For duplicate/blocking guards, filter by active status and exact asset or option contract so filled, canceled, rejected, expired, or error orders do not block new entries.
- After submit_order(order), prefer tracking the submitted order identifier and calling self.get_order(order.identifier) for same-order checks. Broad broker order lists used by self.get_orders(...) can lag briefly after submit, so call self.sleep(..., process_pending_orders=True) first if the strategy must use filtered self.get_orders(...) immediately after submitting.
- After cancel_order(order), process pending orders and refresh self.get_order(order.identifier). is_canceled() and is_active() can classify CANCELLING/pending-cancel as inactive; neither alone confirms cancellation or removes fill exposure. Reconcile broker terminal state, actual fills and residual quantity before clearing the affected order blocker or accepted exit intent. Unrelated assets may continue.
- get_cash() and get_portfolio_value() can return None if the live broker balance refresh fails. Do not treat None as 0; log it and skip sizing/trading decisions that require that value.
- Lumibot strategy code should be broker agnostic, meaning that it should not depend on any specific broker or API. The strategy code should only handle the strategy logic and not the broker.
- Only files saved in the current BotSpot revision are packaged for execution. Keep the strategy self-contained within its saved revision. Ordinary saved Python helper modules and configuration files travel with that revision and may be imported/read by main.py. Save every dependency with the existing file tools, retain the complete revision, and read the final files back. Never depend on an unsaved local path or assume an external file exists. A tested lifecycle helper belongs in an ordinary saved module when its integration requires one.
- Try to avoid using too much date calculations if you don't need them, calculating and comparing dates can be very slow
- Crypto futuresd can have fractional quantities, so for example you can buy 0.5 BTC or 0.1 ETH or 0.01 SOL, etc for Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO_FUTURE. 
- Use self.get_quote(asset) to get bid/ask spreads and detailed market data. Returns a Quote object with .bid, .ask, .mid_price properties. Note: Data.get_quote() (internal) returns a dictionary with OHLCV+bid/ask data. CRITICAL: get_last_price() is trade-only (can be stale) — for options valuation/sizing/spread checks always prefer quote.mid_price (with bid/ask validation).
- Try to avoid using try/except blocks unless absolutely necessary, they can hide errors and make debugging difficult. If you do use them, make sure to log the error message so you can see what went wrong.
- When using cont futures, always use the base symbol (eg. "MNQ" instead of "MNQ1" and "ES" instead of "ES1" or any otehr derivative). Only the base symbol is needed for cont futures, any other derivative will fail because Asset.AssetType.CONT_FUTURE automatically resolves to the base symbol.
- For futures and continuous futures backtests, `get_last_price(asset)` can return `None` even when historical bars and indicators exist for that same asset. Do not let that create a zero-trade smoke. If `get_last_price(...)` is `None`, call `get_historical_prices(asset, lookback, timestep)` and use the latest completed bar close as the reference price for sizing, smoke-entry fallback, and market-order decisions. Log whether the price came from last price or bar close.
- CRITICAL FOR FUTURES: For Asset.AssetType.FUTURE, ALWAYS use the ROOT symbol (e.g., "CL", "ES", "MES") and specify the contract via expiration=... . Do NOT embed month codes / year into Asset.symbol. If you need two different contract months (calendar spread), use two Asset objects with the same root symbol but different expirations.
- CRITICAL ARCHITECTURE RULE: Never assign arbitrary attributes on the strategy instance (self). Do NOT do things like self.name = "...", self.asset = Asset(...), self.quote_asset = Asset(...), self.symbol = "...", etc. These names can collide with Lumibot internals (e.g., self.name) and crash the app or override framework behavior.
- Required pattern: Use self.vars for any state you need to persist between lifecycle methods or restarts (e.g., self.vars.last_signal = "cash"). For temporary values, use local variables. If you need a friendly label for logs, keep it in a local variable or self.vars (e.g., self.vars.strategy_label); never set self.name.
- When you set the parameters, make sure that there's only one spot where they all are, and they should not override each other. For example, what's recommended is to add a parameters = {} dictionary at the top inside of the strategy class. Do not set the parameters again in other places, such as inside of the "if __name__ == "__main__":" area because they will override each other and cause confusion. So just set the parameters once at the top of the strategy class and do not set them again anywhere else.
- Rare-use only: Do NOT implement `tearsheet_custom_metrics(...)` unless the user explicitly asks for strategy-specific tearsheet summary metrics or a client requirement clearly needs non-generic summary rows. Generic reusable metrics belong in QuantStats/LumiBot core. If you use the hook, return only a small dict of unit-clear scalar values; they appear in both `tearsheet.html` and `tearsheet_metrics.json`.
- IMPORTANT: if you are trading Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO_FUTURE then the only way to exit a posotion is to use self.close_position(position.asset). You cannot use self.submit_order() to exit a position for crypto futures, because that will just open a new position on the other side of the trade. So always use self.close_position() to exit a position for crypto futures. If the strategy is trying to exit a position for crypto futures using self.submit_order() for Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO_FUTURE then you should change it to use self.close_position() instead.
- 🚨 PREFER self.indicators FOR TECHNICAL INDICATORS. LumiBot exposes `self.indicators` on every Strategy. It computes from history available at strategy time and reuses identical observed inputs; new or corrected input may require recomputation. Use `self.indicators.<name>(asset, timestep="day", **kwargs)` for the ~130 pandas-ta-classic built-ins (sma, ema, rsi, atr, bbands, macd, adx, stoch, etc.). Single-column indicators return a float; multi-column return an IndicatorRow with attribute access (e.g., `bb.BBL_20_2_0`, `bb.BBU_20_2_0`). For user-defined indicators use `self.indicators.custom("label", fn, asset, timestep="day", **kwargs)` where `fn(df, **kwargs)` receives the full-history DataFrame and returns a Series or DataFrame.
- 🚨 DO NOT hand-roll `df["col"] = df["close"].rolling(...).mean()` or `df["col"] = df["close"].rolling(...).apply(...)` inside on_trading_iteration. Every iteration would recompute the full-history rolling window — on a 13-year daily backtest that is ~1M redundant operations per indicator. Use `self.indicators.sma(asset, length=N)` / `self.indicators.custom(...)` instead. Preserve the requested mathematical convention and history initialization; performance depends on the data path and observed inputs.
- When porting a legacy `compute_indicators(self, df)` helper to `self.indicators`, pass the *same function* directly to `self.indicators.custom("label", self.compute_indicators, asset, timestep="day")`. Do not inline the rolling math into on_trading_iteration. The custom function should accept a DataFrame `df` (the full history), compute derived columns (rolling windows, EMAs, etc.), and return either a Series (single-column indicator) or a DataFrame (multi-column indicator, keyed the same index). `self.indicators.custom(...)` returns the latest row at the current bar; access columns via attribute (`row.median_200`) or key (`row["median_200"]`). Returns None if the data source has no bars yet.
- `self.indicators` caches results per (asset, timestep, name, kwargs). Different parameter sets (e.g., length=20 vs length=50) produce distinct memoized entries automatically; you do not need to manage cache invalidation. The memo transparently recomputes when the underlying bar series grows, so routed/live backtests stay correct as more bars are prefetched.
- Return values from `self.indicators`: `None` when the data source has no bars for (asset, timestep); `NaN` (or a row of NaNs) when the indicator hasn't accumulated enough bars yet. Guard with `if value is None: return` followed by `if pd.isna(value): return` for multi-column rows check individual columns.

- Always include Google-style docstrings with Args sections for every function, especially @agent_tool decorated functions. The docstring becomes part of the tool description the agent sees.
- Default generated strategies to `self.sleeptime = "1D"` unless the user explicitly asks for intraday/high-frequency trading or a specific shorter cadence. Daily cadence keeps normal backtests fast and inexpensive. Do not use `30M`, `15M`, `5M`, or seconds as a silent default.
- For short live order deadlines, cadence is not a preemption mechanism. Reconcile tracked deadlines first, return after timed submits, batch independent reads, cache slow chain/candidate data with bounded freshness, and resume large scans across wall-clock-bounded iterations.
- When the user wants AI-powered or non-deterministic trading, use the AI agents component. Built-in tools are included automatically. Add @agent_tool only when the user names a real external provider/API, uploads reference code, or explicitly asks for a custom integration; do not invent generic news APIs or new API-key requirements. For news, prefer `BuiltinTools.news.alpaca_news()` with the scan-first (`include_content=False`) then full-read (`include_content=True`) workflow. AI agents require one API key matching their model provider.
- 🚨 ABSOLUTE BAN: NEVER add `from __future__ import annotations` to ANY generated code! This import makes backtests CRASH and strategies FAIL to run. It is completely unnecessary and will break everything. Do NOT use it. Ever.
- Options performance reminder: avoid scanning large strike lists and calling `get_greeks()` per strike to “hunt” a target delta; this can flood the downloader queue. Prefer `OptionsHelper.find_strike_for_delta(...)` (keyword args) for delta-based strike selection.
- CRITICAL FOR OPTIONS FEES: When backtesting options strategies, ALWAYS use `TradingFee(per_contract_fee=0.65)` (not flat_fee). The per_contract_fee is multiplied by order quantity (e.g., 40 contracts x $0.65 = $26.00 per leg). Using flat_fee=0.65 would charge only $0.65 total per order regardless of size, which is wrong and drastically undercounts commissions.
- CRITICAL: When selecting option expiries, NEVER manually select from chains - ALWAYS use OptionsHelper.get_expiration_on_or_after_date() or find_next_valid_option() because not every option expiry has tradeable data (options may not exist yet during backtesting)
- If you set the quote asset for a cryptocurrency asset then make sure you set it for both backtesting and live trading. The backtest() function should be called with quote_asset set, as well as the initialisation of the strategy in live trading.
- Do not EVER do things "for demonstration purposes only" all code must always be fully functional and ready to run as is.
- Almost every strategy should have at least one marker and one line to show the strategy on the chart, so try to add them when possible. Remember that add_marker should be used for events that happen infrequently, like a buy or sell signal, while add_line should be used for things that are continuous like moving averages or indicators. ALWAYS pass the asset parameter when you have an Asset object for the indicator.
- Never add markers on every trading iteration! this creates a HUGE mess. Use add_ohlc for price candles (bars), add_line for continuous single-value indicators like moving averages, and add_marker for infrequent events like buy/sell signals. For example: self.add_ohlc("SPY", open=o, high=h, low=l, close=c, dt=dt, asset=spy_asset), self.add_line("SPY_SMA20", sma_value, dt=dt, asset=spy_asset), self.add_marker("buy_signal", price, color="green", symbol="arrow-up", dt=dt, asset=spy_asset).
- It's worth repeating: add_marker() should be rare, never on every iteration because it will crash the chart. Charts cannot handle too many markers, so use them sparingly. Use add_ohlc() for price bars and add_line() for continuous indicators.
- Chart panel rule: when you have `asset=...`, keep overlays on that asset chart and avoid `plot_name` by default. Use `plot_name` only for intentionally separate panes (RSI/MACD/Stochastic/etc.), and keep pane count small unless the user explicitly asks for many panes.
- CRITICAL: add_ohlc(), add_line(), and add_marker() do NOT have a 'text' parameter - using 'text=' will cause a TypeError! The correct signatures are:
  - add_ohlc(name, open, high, low, close, color=None, detail_text=None, dt=None, asset=None) - Example: self.add_ohlc("SPY", open=o, high=h, low=l, close=c, detail_text="SPY Price", asset=my_asset)
  - add_line(name, value, color=None, style='solid', width=None, detail_text=None, dt=None, asset=None) - Example: self.add_line("SMA_20", sma_value, color="blue", detail_text="20-day moving average", asset=my_asset)
  - add_marker(name, value, color=None, symbol='circle', size=None, detail_text=None, dt=None, asset=None) - Example: self.add_marker("Buy Signal", price, color="green", symbol="arrow-up", detail_text="Bullish crossover", asset=my_asset)
  - Use 'name' (first param) for the label and 'detail_text' for hover text. There is NO 'text' parameter!
- RETROACTIVE INDICATORS (PREFERRED): For most charting (support/resistance, trendlines, patterns, signals), draw retroactively using the dt parameter. Use `for dt in self.get_historical_prices(asset, 30, "day").df.index: self.add_line(...)` or store datetimes in self.vars and loop back. Only draw per-iteration for simple deterministic indicators like EMAs/RSI.
- When a value should stay constant across time (support levels, detected patterns), LOCK it in self.vars when first detected and keep outputting that same locked value. Recalculating each iteration causes jagged/noisy visuals.
- 🚨 UPGRADE TO add_ohlc(): If you see a strategy using add_line() to track raw asset prices (e.g., close prices), you should STRONGLY RECOMMEND upgrading to add_ohlc(). The add_ohlc() method provides full candlestick visualization (open, high, low, close) which is far more valuable for understanding price action than a simple line chart. This upgrade significantly improves the user's ability to analyze their strategy. Unless the user explicitly declines, always suggest this upgrade when refining strategies that use add_line() for price data.
- Remember the options are x100, so you have to multiply the price by 100 to get the correct price for the option. For example, if the price of the option is 0.5, then the price of the option is actually 50 dollars. So you have to multiply the price by 100 to get the correct price for the option. So far example if I tell you to use 10% of the account and the option is trading at 1.50 and you have 100,000 in the account, then you have to use 10% of 100,000 which is 10,000 and then divide that by 100 to get the correct amount of options to buy. So in this case you would buy 10,000 / 1.50 / 100 = 66.67 options. So you would buy 66 options.
- Remember that get_last_price() can return None and does so pretty often so you should always check if the price is None before using it. Also remember it is the last trade (can be stale) — for options and thin markets prefer get_quote() and validate bid/ask before using mid_price.
- CRITICAL FOR OPTIONS: get_greeks() can return None when option price data is unavailable (e.g., illiquid options with no recent trades or quotes). ALWAYS check if greeks is None before accessing values like delta, gamma, theta, vega. Use a guard pattern: `greeks = self.get_greeks(option_asset); if greeks is not None: delta = greeks.get("delta"); # use delta here`. Do NOT use `return` when Greeks is None - that would block the entire strategy from continuing.
- IMPORTANT: Remember that you need to set_market("24/7") in intialize for any crypto bot to work properly. Without this the bot will stop trading at 4pm EST which is wrong for crypto.
- So that means strategies for BTC or ETH, or any other crypto coin MUST USE set_market("24/7") in the initialize method. For backtesting, prefer datasource_class=None so LumiBot can resolve the configured provider from the environment. If the user explicitly requests a direct provider binding, PolygonDataBacktesting or CcxtBacktesting are valid explicit choices. If the user does not specify a market then you should set it to "24/7" by default.
- For BTC/USD, ETH/USD, or stablecoin-quoted spot crypto, create the crypto `Asset` from the base coin only, for example `Asset("BTC", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.CRYPTO)`, and pass/set a separate USD quote asset when needed. Never use pair strings such as `BTC-USD`, `BTC/USD`, or `BTCUSD` as a spot crypto asset symbol.
- If you are instructed to do something "before the market opens", implement it in the before_market_opens lifecycle method and store any needed state in self.vars so it can be accessed later in on_trading_iteration.
- If you are instructed to do something "during trading hours" or "during market hours", implement it in the on_trading_iteration lifecycle method.
- Be verbose with logs (self.log_message()) around trading decisions, data fetches, and guard clauses so we can trace each branch.
- When buying crypto make sure that you allow fractions of the asset for a few decimal places, lumibot will correct it if you use too many decimals, but if you use too few decimals then it may not buy the asset at all. So for example if you want to buy 0.5464 BTC then you should use 0.5464 and not 0.546 or 0.55 or 0.5, because lumibot will correct it to the nearest decimal place and it may not buy the asset at all. So try to use as many decimal places as possible when buying crypto. 
- self.log_message() can only use the colors white, red, green, blue, or yellow. Do not use any other colors or it will not work!
- Seriously make sure you are verbose with logs. If  you are not going to trade then log it (this is important so people know why the bot is not trading), if you are going to trade then log it (this is important so people know what the bot is doing), if you are going to sleep then log it (this is important so people know why the bot is not trading), if you are going to do something then log it (this is important so people know what the bot is doing). Aim for 2-3 informative messages per decision block, not copy-pasted spam.
- TRADING FEES BY ASSET CLASS: Use the correct TradingFee type for each asset class. For OPTIONS, use `TradingFee(per_contract_fee=0.65)` (IBKR standard $0.65/contract/leg; this is multiplied by order quantity, so a 40-contract order costs $26). For FUTURES, use `TradingFee(per_contract_fee=0.85)` (standard) or `TradingFee(per_contract_fee=0.50)` (micros). For STOCKS, use `TradingFee(percent_fee=0.001)` (0.1% of order value). NEVER use flat_fee for options or futures because flat_fee is a fixed amount per ORDER regardless of contract count, which massively undercounts commissions on multi-contract trades.
- Strategy logic must be broker-agnostic: never include broker API keys, never call broker SDK/REST directly, and never implement broker-specific order semantics inside Strategy methods.
- It is OK for the `if __name__ == "__main__":` harness to set `datasource_class=None` and let the environment choose the real backtesting provider. Only hardcode a datasource class when the user explicitly requests a provider or the strategy truly depends on a direct local datasource such as PandasDataBacktesting.
- Futures backtests should also default to datasource_class=None unless the user explicitly requests a direct provider binding such as InteractiveBrokersRESTBacktesting or DataBentoDataBacktesting.
- Futures symbols are roots (not spot tickers). IBKR/CME crypto examples: Bitcoin micro `MBT` vs standard `BRR`; Ether micro `MET` vs standard `ETHUSDRR`.
- If you are trading SPX options or NDX options, make sure to use the correct underlying asset, which is an Asset object that represents the index itself (e.g., SPX or NDX) and not a stock or ETF that tracks the index. Asset("SPX", asset_type=AssetType.INDEX) for example is the underlying asset for SPX options, not an ETF or stock
- VIX is an index, not a stock: ALWAYS fetch it as `Asset("VIX", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.INDEX)` (never `^VIX`), and treat `get_last_price(...)` returning None/NaN as “VIX unavailable” (log it and skip/disable the VIX filter for that iteration).
- If you need very up to date data then get_historical_prices() is not a good choice, you should use get_last_price() or get_quote(). The get_historical_prices is for HISTORICAL data and is usually delayed by up to a minute, it does not provide not up to the second prices. get_last_price and get_quote are designed to be more real-time and provide the latest available prices.
- If a user asks you to get historical data and make sure that it is up-to-date or has to be very timely, then you might want to consider using a combination of the get_historical_prices method along with the `get_last_price` or `get_quote` method together where you would have to build kind of your own thing where you're using historical data along with current data. 
- If a user wants faster price action or complains that the speed is too slow in terms of trading, then a likely culprit could be that you're using `get_historical_prices` instead of `get_quote` or `get_last_price`, which are much faster and up-to-date with most brokers. They will get data in between bars, whereas `get_historical_prices` has a speed limit of 1 minute bars at best.

Finite SMA history (verified LumiBot 4.6.32): use `self.indicators.sma(asset, length=N)` and `self.indicators.sma(asset, length=N, offset=1)` for current and prior values. Do not wrap ordinary built-in SMAs in a custom indicator just to combine those values. The built-in requests its finite window; recursive/custom calculations retain their existing initialization contract. Keep completed-bar timing, corporate-action handling and missing required-input checks.

--------------------------------------------------------------
PERPLEXITYHELPER COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------------------

A helper for querying Perplexity’s API via an OpenAI-compatible client.
It supports two types of queries:
	•	Financial news queries: Returns structured financial news data—ideal for getting current news such as earnings reports, analyst recommendations, and other market-moving events.
	•	General queries: Returns structured responses based on a provided (or default) JSON schema, which is useful for finding symbols that match specific criteria, identifying volatile stocks, or retrieving other trading-related insights.

This component is especially valuable because it can perform live searches to gather real-time information, ensuring your strategy has access to the latest data when making decisions.

Constructor
----------------
class PerplexityHelper:
    def __init__(self, api_key: str) -> None

Key Methods
------------
	1.	execute_financial_news_query(self, user_query: str) -> dict
	•	Description:
Executes a financial news query by constructing a prompt that adheres to a strict JSON schema, sending the query to the Perplexity API, cleaning the response, and returning structured financial news data.
	•	Expected Data Structure:
        {
            "query": "<string, echo the user's query>",
            "analysis_summary": "<string, a concise summary of the news findings>",
            "items": [
                {
                "symbol": "<string, e.g. 'AAPL' or 'TSLA'>",
                "asset_type": "<string, e.g. 'stock', 'crypto', 'index'>",
                "headline": "<string, a brief headline summarizing the news>",
                "confidence": <integer, 0-10>,
                "sentiment_score": <integer, -10 to 10>,
                "popularity_metric": <integer, non-negative count>,
                "volume_of_messages": <integer, optional>,
                "magnitude": <integer, 0-10>,
                "type_of_news": "<string, optional, e.g. 'earnings', 'ipo', 'macro'>",
                "price_targets": {
                    "low": <float, optional>,
                    "high": <float, optional>,
                    "average": <float, optional>
                },
                "additional_info": {
                    "sector": "<string, optional>",
                    "recent_events": "<string, optional>",
                    "notable_executive_actions": "<string, optional>",
                    "macro_support": "<string, optional>",
                    "related_tickers": ["<string, list of similar tickers>"],
                    "external_links": ["<string, URL>"]
                }
                }
            ]
        }

    2.	execute_general_query(self, user_query: str, custom_schema=None, model: str = "sonar") -> dict
	•	Description:
Executes a general query using either a default or a custom JSON schema. This method is ideal for retrieving general market insights, symbol lists, or other trading-related data.
	•	Expected Data Structure (Default Schema which can be customized by providing a custom_schema):
        {
            "query": "<string, echo the user's query>",
            "response_summary": "<string, brief answer (1-3 sentences)>",
            "detailed_response": "<string, optional extended details>",
            "symbols": ["<string, list of relevant symbols>"]
        }

HOW TO LOAD AND USE THE PERPLEXITYHELPER COMPONENT IN YOUR STRATEGY
--------------------------------------------------------------

	1.	Import the component:

from lumibot.components.perplexity_helper import PerplexityHelper

	2.	Instantiate the helper in your strategy’s initialize() method:

def initialize(self):
    self.perplexity_helper = PerplexityHelper(api_key="your_api_key_here")

    3.	Call its functions in a lifecycle method (e.g., on_trading_iteration):
def on_trading_iteration(self):
    # Example for a financial news query
    news_query = "What are the latest earnings reports for major tech companies?"
    news_data = self.perplexity_helper.execute_financial_news_query(news_query)
    self.log_message(f"News Query Result: {news_data}")

    # Example for a general query with the default schema
    general_query = "Which stocks are showing high volatility today?"
    general_data = self.perplexity_helper.execute_general_query(general_query)
    self.log_message(f"General Query Result: {general_data}")

Additional Considerations
-------------------------
	•	API Key Setup:
Ensure you have a valid Perplexity API key. It can be provided directly when instantiating the helper or set as the environment variable PERPLEXITY_API_KEY.
	•	Real-Time Information:
The PerplexityHelper is highly effective at retrieving current, real-time data. Whether you need up-to-the-minute earnings reports, analyst insights, or symbol-specific data, this component leverages Perplexity’s search capabilities to keep your strategy informed with the latest market developments.

# Fast and Responsive LumiBot Strategies

A LumiBot strategy is slow for a small number of reasons: it runs more
iterations than it needs, it recomputes the same thing every iteration, it reads
data one symbol at a time, or it blocks the iteration while waiting on the
broker. This skill shows how to find which one applies and fix it without
changing what the strategy trades.

The rule that governs everything here: **speed changes how data is acquired and
when work happens, never the trading policy.** Keep the same universe order,
thresholds, quantities, formulas, cooldowns, order guards and fallbacks. A
"faster" version that skips symbols, drops a guard or suppresses eligible trades
is a different strategy, not an optimization.

Related skills: `lumibot-api-reference` for exact signatures,
`lumibot-strategy-building` for the overall build and backtest workflow,
`options-strategies` for options-specific logic, `lumibot-indicators` for
indicator details, `lumibot-ai-agents` for AI-agent strategies.

## References in this skill

Load a reference with the `skills` tool (action=get,
name=fast-lumibot-strategies, reference=references/<file>):

| Load | When |
|---|---|
| `references/scanner-performance.md` | A scan over many symbols or option contracts is slow; you need to batch quotes, cut repeated account/order reads, and keep every guard and price fallback intact. Includes the full two-level scan pattern and a verification checklist. |
| `references/quote-snapshot-example.py` | You are adding batched bid/ask reads with `get_quotes`. A complete, bounded, failure-isolating reader to adapt into the strategy file (it is not an installed LumiBot module). |
| `references/fast-order-management.md` | Cancel-after-N-seconds, immediate hedge or pair legs after a fill, late fills during cancellation, duplicate hedge prevention, manual-cancel and restart recovery, broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket. Includes a complete state-machine pattern and the cases to test. |

## Step 1: find where the time goes

Do not guess. Before changing code:

1. Read the strategy (`get_file` on BotSpot) and list what each iteration does:
   how many symbols, how many `get_historical_prices`, `get_quote`,
   `get_last_price`, `get_chains`, `get_greeks`, `get_orders`, `get_positions`
   and `get_cash` calls, and any loops, sleeps or retries.
2. Check the cadence: `self.sleeptime` and the backtest window. Iterations times
   per-iteration work is the total cost.
3. Look at the logs of a real run (`get_backtest_logs`) for repeated work,
   timeouts, retries and skipped-entry reasons.
4. Classify the problem:
   - too many iterations (cadence), go to Step 2;
   - repeated computation, go to Step 3;
   - serial data reads, go to Step 4 and the scanner reference;
   - blocking order handling or missed deadlines, go to Step 6 and the order
     reference.

After the change, run the same backtest window again and compare (Step 8).

## Step 2: choose the right cadence

- Default to `self.sleeptime = "1D"` unless the strategy genuinely makes intraday
  decisions. A minute cadence runs hundreds of times more iterations than daily,
  and every iteration pays for its data reads. Use `"1M"`, `"5M"` or `"15M"` only
  when the logic needs it, and seconds (`"10S"`, `"1S"`) only for live order
  management.
- Minute-level history is limited (often about two years), so minute backtests
  must use shorter windows anyway.
- `sleeptime` is the gap after an iteration finishes. It never interrupts a
  running iteration. A one-second sleeptime does nothing for a scan that takes
  six seconds; the scan itself has to get shorter or be split (Step 5).
- Work that only needs to happen once a day belongs in `before_market_opens`
  (watchlists, chain lookups, daily resets), with the results stored in
  `self.vars`. It should not run on every intraday iteration.
- Crypto strategies run around the clock with `set_market("24/7")`, which also
  multiplies iterations. Pick the slowest cadence the logic tolerates.

## Step 3: stop recomputing the same thing

**Indicators.** Hand-rolled rolling windows recompute the entire history every
iteration:

```python
# Slow: recomputes the whole series on every iteration
df = self.get_historical_prices(asset, 300, "day").df
sma = df["close"].rolling(200).mean().iloc[-1]

# Fast: computed once over the series, cached, looked up per bar
sma = self.indicators.sma(asset, length=200, timestep="day")
if sma is None or pd.isna(sma):
    return
```

`self.indicators` caches per asset, timestep and parameters, and refreshes
automatically when new bars arrive. For custom math, pass the function to
`self.indicators.custom("label", fn, asset, timestep="day")`; `fn(df)` receives
the full history and returns a Series (scalar result) or a DataFrame
(IndicatorRow result). On indicator-heavy daily backtests this change alone
often cuts runtime substantially. Make the migration behavior-preserving: same
algorithm, smoothing, warmup and decision timing; compare values on a few bars
before replacing an existing calculation.

**Option chains and contracts.** `get_chains` is slow. Cache it once per day (or
per session) in `self.vars`, keyed by date:

```python
today = self.get_datetime().date()
if getattr(self.vars, "chains_date", None) != today:
    self.vars.chains = self.get_chains(underlying)
    self.vars.chains_date = today
chains = self.vars.chains
```

Store the full selected `Asset` objects (strike, expiry, right included), not just
symbols, so later iterations do not refetch or rebuild them. Cache the selected
expiry and strikes and recompute only when the underlying has moved materially
or the date changed.

**Delta hunting.** Never loop `get_greeks()` over a strike list to find a target
delta. Each call is a data request, so a 100-strike loop is 100 requests per
iteration. Use `OptionsHelper.find_strike_for_delta(...)` (keyword arguments,
`underlying_price` required) and `get_expiration_on_or_after_date(...)` with
`underlying_asset=...`.

**Static values.** Levels that should not change once detected (support,
resistance, a pattern's anchor) belong in `self.vars` the first time they are
found. Recomputing them every iteration costs time and makes charts jagged.

**Date math and charting.** Avoid unnecessary date calculations inside tight
loops. Plot price with one `add_ohlc` per bar and indicators with `add_line`; add
markers only for rare events. Markers on every iteration bloat the output and can
break the chart.

## Step 4: batch data calls

Replace per-symbol loops with the batched methods:

| Instead of | Use |
|---|---|
| `get_historical_prices` in a loop | `get_historical_prices_for_assets(assets, length, timestep)` returns `{asset: Bars or None}` and fetches in parallel |
| `get_last_price` in a loop | `get_last_prices(assets)` (trade prices only) |
| `get_quote` in a loop (bid/ask decisions) | `get_quotes(assets)` (LumiBot 4.6.19+), returns `{asset: Quote or None}` |

```python
bars_by_asset = self.get_historical_prices_for_assets(assets, 60, "day")
for asset in assets:
    bars = bars_by_asset.get(asset)
    if bars is None or bars.df.empty:
        self.log_message(f"{asset.symbol}: no bars, skipping", color="yellow")
        continue
    ...
```

Things to know about batching quotes:

- `get_last_prices` returns last trades. It is not a bid/ask snapshot and cannot
  replace a bid/ask or midpoint formula.
- Native batching depends on the data source. Some sources send one request per
  batch (Schwab accepts up to 50 symbols per request); others fall back to
  individual reads. Check before claiming fewer network requests.
- `get_quote` swallows read errors and returns None; direct `get_quotes` can
  raise for the whole batch when one member is malformed or a request fails.
  Wrapping it in `try/except: continue` silently drops healthy contracts. Use the
  bounded, failure-isolating reader in `references/quote-snapshot-example.py`.
- A missing quote stays missing for that scan. Do not let an old helper refetch
  it one by one, which brings the serial loop back.
- Pass the snapshot quote into every consumer that would otherwise fetch again,
  including `OptionsHelper.evaluate_option_market(option, max_spread_pct=..., quote=quote)`.

For live freshness, `get_last_price` and `get_quote` return the latest tick and
are faster than requesting historical bars, which are at best one-minute bars and
can lag. If a live strategy feels sluggish because it calls
`get_historical_prices` for the current price, switch the current-price read to
`get_quote` or `get_last_price` and keep history for indicators.

## Step 5: scanners over many symbols

For a basket scan, split the work into two levels and make each read only where
the original decision needed it:

1. Per symbol, in the original order: keep the symbol-level guard (for example
   an active-order check) exactly where it was.
2. Select candidate contracts from cached chain data, then read their quotes in
   one bounded batch.
3. Evaluate price and eligibility from the batch first. Only for a candidate that
   is still viable, refresh orders and run the original exact-contract guard.
4. Submit using the existing logic and stop or continue as the original did.

This removes both common hot paths (serial option quotes and per-candidate
account reads) without moving guards. The full pattern, the validation and price
fallback rules, and a verification checklist are in
`references/scanner-performance.md`. Read it before editing a real scanner.

When a scan cannot finish quickly (very large universe, slow provider, or an
order deadline in flight), chunk it with a resumable cursor and a wall-clock
budget instead of scanning everything in one iteration:

```python
import time

def _run_one_bounded_scan_step(self):
    universe = self.parameters["symbols"]
    cursor = getattr(self.vars, "scan_cursor", 0)
    budget_seconds = float(self.parameters.get("scan_budget_seconds", 2.0))
    started = time.monotonic()

    while cursor < len(universe):
        if time.monotonic() - started > budget_seconds:
            break                        # resume here on the next iteration
        symbol = universe[cursor]
        cursor += 1
        if self._handle_symbol(symbol):  # existing per-symbol logic; True if it traded
            break
    if cursor >= len(universe):
        cursor = 0                       # full pass complete
        self.vars.last_full_scan_at = self.get_datetime().isoformat()
    self.vars.scan_cursor = cursor
```

Use `time.monotonic()` for elapsed-time budgets. Bound every provider retry per
call and per iteration, and log when a pass was incomplete so nobody mistakes an
unfinished scan for "no opportunities".

## Step 6: fast and safe order handling

The iteration must never block waiting for the broker. Core rules:

- Do not `while`-loop until an order fills, and never use `time.sleep()` (use
  `self.sleep(...)` only for short, bounded waits). Store deadlines and order ids
  in `self.vars` and check them next iteration, or use the resident wait pattern
  in the order reference for second-level deadlines.
- Reconcile pending orders and deadlines **before** starting a fresh scan. After
  submitting an order with a short deadline, return instead of continuing a long
  scan in the same iteration.
- React to fills in `on_filled_order` / `on_partially_filled_order` (the fast
  path), and keep a reconciliation fallback in `on_trading_iteration` for missed
  callbacks. Share one idempotency record keyed by the original order identifier
  so the callback and the fallback cannot both place a hedge.
- Use `self.get_order(order.identifier)` for an exact order. Do not poll it in a
  tight loop, and do not use broad `get_orders()` scans on a deadline-critical
  path. On rate-limit errors (HTTP 429) back off, honoring `Retry-After`.
- `cancel_order` is a request. `CANCELLING`/pending-cancel, a missing read, a
  timeout or a cancel exception are all unresolved, not terminal. Keep the
  affected symbol or pair blocked until the broker confirms a terminal state and
  any required hedge is resolved.
- Use `Order.OrderStatus.ERROR` for rejections; there is no `REJECTED` status.
- Prefer broker-native OTO/OCO/bracket orders when the relationship fits (for
  example take-profit plus stop-loss). Use a strategy-managed state machine only
  for flows a native order class cannot express, such as a custom stock hedge
  after an option fill or a strict cancel-after-N-seconds.
- Second-level deadlines need a continuously running process. On BotSpot, use an
  always-on deployment or a schedule window that covers the whole trading
  period; a one-shot scheduled run cannot own a sub-minute deadline.

`references/fast-order-management.md` has the complete cancel-after-N-seconds
plus immediate-hedge state machine, the deadline architecture, restart
recovery, and the list of cases to test before trusting it with real money.

## Step 7: backtest speed

- Start with a short window (a few months of daily bars) to prove the strategy
  runs and trades, then extend. Long minute-level backtests are the slowest kind.
- Keep the universe as small as the idea allows while iterating; widen it once
  the logic is right.
- Use daily cadence for daily logic. An intraday cadence on a daily idea only
  multiplies work.
- Use `self.indicators`, cached chains and batched reads (Steps 3 and 4). They
  help backtests as much as live trading.
- Avoid live web or API calls in backtests unless they are replay-safe or cached.
- AI-agent strategies call a model on every simulated iteration. They are the
  slowest backtests: keep the first run to about a week of daily iterations and a
  small universe (see `lumibot-ai-agents`).
- Options backtests depend on per-contract data; selecting contracts through
  `OptionsHelper` and caching them avoids requesting data for contracts that do
  not exist or are never traded.
- Log decisions and reasons, but avoid dumping large DataFrames every iteration.

## Step 8: measure and report honestly

On BotSpot:

1. Save the change (`patch_file` or `replace_file`) and read it back with
   `get_file` to confirm every caller uses the new path.
2. Run the same window as before with `start_backtest`, track it with
   `backtest_status`, and compare runtimes.
3. Check `get_backtest_logs` and the trade output (`get_backtest_artifact`,
   `query_csv`) to confirm the strategy still makes the same decisions on the
   same data. Any change in trades needs an explanation.

Report what you measured (runtime, number of requests if logged, iterations) and
describe the saved code accurately. If a hot path is still unchanged, say so. Do
not claim a speedup you did not measure, and never present speed as evidence that
the strategy will make money.

Live deployment and any real-money order always need the user's explicit
approval on botspot.trade. Nothing in this skill is investment advice.

# LumiBot examples: AI agents

Patterns for LumiBot AI agents: minimal agent, research plus trader team, bull/bear committee, built-in news tool, and a custom `@agent_tool`. Replace `<model id>` with the model the user picked (see `references/components-overview.md`, AI agents section, for model ids and keys). For the full design guide load the `lumibot-ai-agents` skill.

These snippets show methods from inside a `Strategy` subclass (`self` is the strategy). Imports such as `Asset`, `Order`, `TradingFee`, `timedelta` and `pd` are assumed. Examples are illustrations of the API, not trading recommendations.

```python
# Example - Minimal built-in-tools AI agent:
# This example shows the smallest useful pattern for creating and running a LumiBot AI agent
# with only built-in tools. Built-in tools are included by default -- no explicit listing needed.

def initialize(self):
    self.agents.create(
        name="research",
        default_model="<model id>",
        system_prompt="Use LumiBot tools and return a short summary.",
    )

def on_trading_iteration(self):
    self.agents["research"].run(
        context={"symbol": "SPY", "current_datetime": self.get_datetime().isoformat()}
    )


# Example - Strict minimal AI-owned trading team:
# Every AI-owned trading strategy keeps research separate from the sole terminal
# risk/trader. Do not collapse this to one trading-enabled agent.

def initialize(self):
    # Default to daily cadence for backtest speed/cost unless the user explicitly asks for intraday.
    self.sleeptime = "1D"
    self.agents.create(
        name="researcher",
        default_model="<model id>",
        allow_trading=False,
        system_prompt="Research opportunities and return a bounded evidence packet. Never trade.",
    )
    self.agents.create(
        name="risk_trader",
        default_model="<model id>",
        allow_trading=True,
        system_prompt="Revalidate evidence and account risk, then trade or hold.",
    )

def on_trading_iteration(self):
    research = self.agents["researcher"].run()
    self.agents["risk_trader"].run(context={"research": research.summary})


# Example - Simple leveraged ETF AI trading team:
# Use this shape when the user asks for an AI trading team that should actively
# pick among a defined universe. The universe includes bullish and inverse
# leveraged ETFs, so the team can express risk-on or risk-off views without
# short selling. Keep on_trading_iteration thin: agents debate, then the trader
# agent handles orders.

parameters = {
    "universe": ["TQQQ", "SQQQ", "UPRO", "SPXU", "UDOW", "SDOW", "TNA", "TZA", "TECL", "TECS", "SOXL", "SOXS", "WEBL", "WEBS", "FAS", "FAZ", "LABU", "LABD", "ERX", "ERY", "GUSH", "DRIP", "DRN", "DRV", "TMF", "TMV", "NUGT", "DUST"],
}

def initialize(self):
    self.sleeptime = "1D"
    self.agents.create(
        name="researcher",
        default_model="<model id>",
        allow_trading=False,
        system_prompt="Rank the ETFs by upside. Be direct.",
    )
    self.agents.create(
        name="bull",
        default_model="<model id>",
        allow_trading=False,
```

```python
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This example shows how to compute a derived OHLC series (Heikin Ashi) and plot it.
# Use self.vars to persist previous HA values between iterations.

import math

asset = Asset("SPY", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.STOCK)
bars = self.get_historical_prices(asset, 2, "day")
if bars is not None:
    df = bars.df
    prev = df.iloc[-2]
    cur = df.iloc[-1]

    ha_close = (cur["open"] + cur["high"] + cur["low"] + cur["close"]) / 4.0
    prev_ha_close = (prev["open"] + prev["high"] + prev["low"] + prev["close"]) / 4.0
    prev_ha_open = (prev["open"] + prev["close"]) / 2.0
    ha_open = (prev_ha_open + prev_ha_close) / 2.0
    ha_high = max(cur["high"], ha_open, ha_close)
    ha_low = min(cur["low"], ha_open, ha_close)

    if all(math.isfinite(float(x)) for x in [ha_open, ha_high, ha_low, ha_close]):
        self.add_ohlc(
            "Heikin Ashi",
            open=ha_open,
            high=ha_high,
            low=ha_low,
            close=ha_close,
            detail_text="Heikin Ashi candles",
            asset=asset,
        )
```

```python
# Example - Getting strike prices for a stock option:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This example demonstrates how to find valid option strikes for a target expiration date,
# handling cases where the desired expiration might not be available.

# Retrieve the current price of PLTR stock.
pltr_asset = Asset("PLTR", asset_type=Asset.AssetType.STOCK)
current_price = self.get_last_price(pltr_asset)
if current_price is None:
    self.log_message(f"{pltr_asset.symbol} price data unavailable. Skipping trade.", color="red")
    return

# Use self.get_datetime() instead of datetime.now() to avoid using datetime.now()
target_expiration_dt = self.get_datetime() + timedelta(days=30)
target_expiration_date = target_expiration_dt.date()
target_expiration_str = target_expiration_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

# Retrieve option chain for PLTR to determine valid strikes.
chains_res = self.get_chains(pltr_asset)
if not chains_res:
    self.log_message(f"Option chains data for {pltr_asset.symbol} unavailable. Skipping trade.", color="red")
    return
call_chains = chains_res.get("Chains", {}).get("CALL")
if not call_chains:
    self.log_message(f"Call option chains data for {pltr_asset.symbol} unavailable. Skipping trade.", color="red")
    return

# Check if the target expiration exists; if not, select the closest available expiration.
if target_expiration_str in call_chains:
    expiration_str = target_expiration_str
    expiration_date = target_expiration_date
else:
    # Convert available expiration strings to date objects for comparison.
    available_expirations = []
    for exp_str in call_chains.keys():
        try:
            exp_date = self.get_datetime().__class__.strptime(exp_str, "%Y-%m-%d").date()  # using class method for conversion
            available_expirations.append(exp_date)
        except Exception as e:
            self.log_message(f"Error parsing expiration date: {exp_str}, error: {e}", color="red")
    if not available_expirations:
        self.log_message("No valid expiration dates found in option chains.", color="red")
        return
    # Choose the available expiration date that is closest to the target expiration date.
    expiration_date = min(available_expirations, key=lambda x: abs((x - target_expiration_date).days))
    expiration_str = expiration_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    self.log_message(f"Target expiration {target_expiration_str} not available. Using closest available expiration: {expiration_str}", color="yellow")

strikes = call_chains.get(expiration_str)
if not strikes or len(strikes) == 0:
    self.log_message(f"No strikes available for expiration {expiration_str}. Skipping trade.", color="red")
    return
```

"""Bounded public-API quote reads; data acquisition only, never trading policy.

LumiBot 4.6.19+ get_quotes returns exact Asset keys, including None for missing
members. Schwab caps native requests at 50. A failed HTTP request raises
ConnectionError; that type alone does not establish provider-wide downtime.
Malformed members/response contracts can raise ValueError or TypeError during
numeric quote construction. Handle those only at the get_quotes acquisition
boundary; this is not a blanket handler for strategy logic or other exceptions. This
example never calls get_quote as a serial fallback or changes a quote's fields.
It cannot interrupt a blocking broker request. Call it before entering a
short-deadline order lifecycle, or use a provider timeout/control path that meets
the remaining deadline. Acquisition time is not provider quote freshness.
"""

import logging
import math
import time
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Callable

from httpx import HTTPError


QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED = object()


def quote_input(strategy: Any, asset: Any, quote: Any = QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED) -> Any:
    """Preserve a supplied missing quote; only legacy omitted input fetches.

    Adapt an existing price helper's default and acquisition to this pattern,
    retaining its original pricing/fallback calculations after this step.
    None from a snapshot means unavailable, never permission for another read.
    """
    return strategy.get_quote(asset) if quote is QUOTE_NOT_PROVIDED else quote


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class QuoteSnapshot:
    quotes: dict[Any, Any]
    unavailable: dict[Any, str]
    acquired_at: dict[Any, float]
    request_count: int


def read_quote_snapshot(
    strategy: Any,
    assets: list[Any],
    *,
    deadline: float | None,
    max_requests: int | None = None,
    monotonic: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic,
) -> QuoteSnapshot:
    """Read once per valid batch; isolate malformed members within a hard budget.

    Pass an actual armed deadline when time-sensitive work can overlap this
    acquisition. An idle pre-entry scan may explicitly pass None: its finite
    contract/request counts and the SDK's finite HTTP timeout still bound work,
    without inventing a quote-age cutoff or a cursor. None is not appropriate
    when a live cancellation deadline needs interleaved service.

    The default request budget derives from the unique contract count: complete
    binary isolation of N members in B initial batches needs at most 2*N-B
    requests. Idle callers should keep that default, not twice the batch count.
    An explicit tighter budget is allowed for an armed deadline; it can leave
    unresolved members that the caller must not call a completed scan.

    The caller owns existing error/retry policy, quote-age validation and order
    management. Inspect unavailable: provider failure, invalid response and
    exhausted budget do not mean that no market or eligible trade exists.
    Missing members remain missing for this snapshot. Isolate a failed batch
    within the same explicit request/deadline budget instead of declaring every
    unrelated instrument unavailable. Budget exhaustion preserves unread work
    as unresolved, not as a completed no-trade scan. Different providers may not implement native batching, so
    measure actual HTTP work before claiming a speed improvement.
    """
    assets = list(dict.fromkeys(assets))
    if max_requests is None:
        batch_count = (len(assets) + 49) // 50
        max_requests = max(1, 2 * len(assets) - batch_count)
    if type(max_requests) is not int or max_requests < 1:
        raise ValueError('max_requests must be a positive finite integer')
    if deadline is not None and not math.isfinite(deadline):
        raise ValueError('deadline must be a finite monotonic time')
    values = dict.fromkeys(assets)
    unavailable: dict[Any, str] = {}
    acquired_at: dict[Any, float] = {}
    pending = deque(assets[index:index + 50] for index in range(0, len(assets), 50))
    requests = 0
    failed_requests = 0
    while pending:
        reason = 'deadline' if deadline is not None and monotonic() >= deadline else (
            'request_budget' if requests >= max_requests else None)
        if reason:
            for batch in pending:
                unavailable.update(dict.fromkeys(batch, reason))
            break
        batch = pending.popleft()
        requests += 1
        try:
            quotes = strategy.get_quotes(batch)
            if not isinstance(quotes, dict) or any(asset not in quotes for asset in batch):
                raise ValueError('Quote adapter omitted requested members')
        except (ConnectionError, HTTPError, ValueError, TypeError) as exc:
            failed_requests += 1
            logging.getLogger(__name__).warning(
                "Quote batch acquisition failed: %s for %d requested assets; bounded recovery applies",
                type(exc).__name__, len(batch),
            )
            if len(batch) == 1:
                unavailable[batch[0]] = ('request_failed' if isinstance(exc, (ConnectionError, HTTPError))
                                         else 'invalid_response')
            else:
                middle = len(batch) // 2
                pending.appendleft(batch[middle:])
                pending.appendleft(batch[:middle])
            continue
        observed_at = monotonic()
        for asset in batch:
            values[asset] = quotes[asset]
            acquired_at[asset] = observed_at
            if quotes[asset] is None:
                unavailable[asset] = 'missing'
    deferred = sum(reason in {"deadline", "request_budget"} for reason in unavailable.values())
    if failed_requests or deferred:
        logging.getLogger(__name__).warning(
            "Quote acquisition: %d failed quote requests; %d retained quotes, "
            "%d unavailable/unread assets; reasons=%s",
            failed_requests, sum(value is not None for value in values.values()),
            len(unavailable), ",".join(sorted(set(unavailable.values()))) or "recovered",
        )
    return QuoteSnapshot(values, unavailable, acquired_at, requests)

  omitted requested key enters bounded isolation/recovery. Do not refetch
  returned missing values through an old helper's implicit singleton fallback.
- On pinned Schwab 4.6.20, `get_quote` catches quote-read/parser failures and
  returns `None`, while direct `get_quotes` can raise. Handle that boundary for
  every newly batched asset type, including underlying-stock prefetch. A
  `ConnectionError` indicates one failed request, not global provider downtime.
- Retain usable members and observable acquisition failures. A malformed or
  failed member must not hide healthy later candidates. Missing quotes, failed
  requests and unread work are distinct; exhausted budgets are not an empty
  market or a completed no-trade scan. Do not introduce an unbounded serial
  fallback or rotate basket priority to conceal incomplete acquisition.

The reader cannot interrupt a blocking HTTP call. An armed cancellation
deadline must be serviced before starting more acquisition, with an appropriate
provider timeout or bounded continuation. A tighter explicit budget may defer
work, but keep unread work explicit. If scanning happens only before submission,
finish that finite idle scan without inventing a deadline or asking the user
to design the batching algorithm.

Reuse structural chain information for a bounded lifetime. Price freshness is
separate: acquisition time does not prove the provider's quote is current.
Keep existing freshness checks and use a new snapshot for a later decision
phase. Do not add a new numeric quote-age filter during a speed-only edit.
Fetch lazily by underlying/bounded step so loading the entire basket does not
delay its first valid opportunity.

## Finish the saved repair before answering

Read the final saved files and trace the full nonqualifying path plus a
qualifying final symbol. Verify both quote and account-read changes in that
readback, every pre-entry consumer, and the later fresh-price callers. Keep
basket priority, expiry policy, thresholds, quantities, formulas, cooldowns,
Rules, dependencies and unrelated files intact. Leave inherited code/Rules
disagreements for a separate user decision.
Compare the old and saved helper bodies, especially deleted rejection and
fallback branches. Review each changed caller with a missing quote, one-sided
quote and newly visible order, rather than only looking for the new batch call.
Verify that failure handling surrounds acquisition and retains healthy members;
a bare batch call or `except: return` is not the original tolerant read policy.

If a hot path remains unchanged, continue the authorized edit. An answer saying
"the main scan is not fully optimized yet" does not complete this request when
supported APIs and ordinary editing tools remain available. Complete the
implementable refactor; report unavailable live timing separately. No live
broker login or forced backtest is needed merely to save that supported edit.

A failed exact-text patch saved nothing, including earlier operations in that
batch. An ambiguous match is an editable local problem, not a permission or API
blocker. Do not retry that same `oldText` in a larger batch. Read the current
file, identify the intended complete method and use its unique method body or
verified range as above; alternatively replace the complete current file.
Continue the authorized repair through a successful save and final readback.
Do not finish with an apology or a request for permission merely because a patch
was ambiguous. Explain a genuinely denied operation, unsupported API or external
prerequisite precisely when it prevents all supported editing routes.
A newly defined reader with its old serial callers still present is unfinished
plumbing. The entry path and pre-entry preparation must actually pass the
acquired quote to their existing helpers, while later callers that omit it
must retain their fresh-read default. Follow the call sites in the saved file;
neither the helper's presence nor an entrypoint readiness result proves wiring.

Measure complete traversal, qualifying decisions, request counts, data age and
cancellation dispatch separately from broker acknowledgment. Report only the
measurements actually observed. A faster-looking change that skips stocks,
suppresses eligible trades, or leaves the demonstrated hot loops unchanged is
not a successful performance repair.

Describe each changed data path precisely in the final answer. A quote snapshot
supplies market prices; order-state checks use their separate order observation.
If those checks still read fresh orders, say so rather than grouping them under
the reused quote snapshot. Verify each claimed change against its saved caller;
an accurate implementation can still be misrepresented by an overbroad summary.

Recommendations are not descriptions of the final saved implementation. Before
claiming when an order refresh happens, inspect its enclosing branch in the
saved caller. A read that still runs unconditionally once per symbol is not a
candidate-only read, even if candidate-only reads were the proposed plan. Say
that repeated reads were reduced unless the more precise placement is verified.
Do not copy a recommendation or revision-analysis description into the final
summary as though it proves the saved call ordering. Report each claimed
mechanism from the actual saved body, including successful alternatives.
